surviving.title: No private-IP / loopback / link-local / metadata SSRF guard on any scanner outbound HTTP, and unbounded redirect following on most checks
surviving.description: Every scanner HTTP client is built on budget.Transport()/WrapTransport(), which wraps http.DefaultTransport with only an atomic request counter — there is no custom DialContext and no IP filtering (confirmed by grep: no net.ParseIP/IsLoopback/IsPrivate/IsLinkLocal/169.254/metadata anywhere outside comments). The crawler (crawler.go) follows attacker-influenced URLs from robots.txt `Sitemap:` directives (parseRobots, lines 726-732), sitemap `<loc>` entries (fromSitemap, fetched via fetchBody before any host filter — the host filter at lines 807-815 only filters which discovered endpoints are KEPT, not which sitemap docs are FETCHED at line 789), `<script src>` (fromJS resolveURL, line 484), and HTML links. Furthermore the crawler client (NewCrawler, lines 104-112), CORS client (cors.go:25-28) and injection client (injection.go:359-362) do NOT set CheckRedirect, so they follow up to Go's default 10 redirects to any host — including 127.0.0.1, 169.254.169.254 (cloud metadata), and RFC1918 hosts. Only auth.go (line 31) and idor.go (line 30) set http.ErrUseLastResponse. A malicious target (or any page the scanner crawls) can therefore redirect a probe to the cloud metadata endpoint or an internal service.
surviving.impact: When Fendix scans an attacker-influenced or untrusted target (or runs as a hosted/multi-tenant scanning service, which the GH App and `fendix serve` roadmap imply), the target can pivot the scanner into the operator's internal network or cloud metadata service (e.g. http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/) via a 302 redirect or a planted sitemap/robots entry, yielding SSRF and potential cloud-credential theft.
surviving.recommendation: Install a shared transport DialContext that resolves the destination and refuses connections to loopback, link-local (169.254.0.0/16, fe80::/10), unique-local, RFC1918/RFC4193, and 0.0.0.0/multicast ranges (re-check after DNS resolution to defeat DNS rebinding, and re-validate on every redirect hop). Set a CheckRedirect on the crawler/CORS/injection clients that caps redirect count and re-applies the same IP policy to each hop. Make this opt-out only for explicitly local/dev targets.
surviving.verifierReasoning:
All load-bearing claims verified against the actual code.

1) No SSRF guard in the transport. budget.go lines 92-138: budgetTransport.RoundTrip (101-116) only does an atomic counter check then calls b.inner.RoundTrip. WrapTransport/Transport (126-138) wrap http.DefaultTransport with no custom DialContext. Grep for ParseIP/IsLoopback/IsPrivate/IsLinkLocal/169.254/metadata returns zero IP-filtering hits anywhere (all "metadata" hits are unrelated report/webhook code). Confirmed.

2) Redirect handling. grep CheckRedirect/ErrUseLastResponse: ONLY auth.go:31 and idor.go:30 set http.ErrUseLastResponse. The crawler client (crawler.go NewCrawler 103-112), cors.go:25-28, injection.go:359-362, plus configleak/ratelimit/exposure/headers all build &http.Client{} with no CheckRedirect, so they follow Go's default 10 redirects to any host (127.0.0.1, 169.254.169.254, RFC1918). Confirmed.

3) The strongest vector — attacker-influenced fetch of a cross-host URL — is real and reachable in DEFAULT passive mode (orchestrator.go:134-135 runs NewCrawler/CrawlEndpoints unconditionally, NOT behind --enable-active). Chain: fromRobots (crawler.go:144) fetches target /robots.txt; parseRobots (688-735) extracts `Sitemap:` directives as raw absolute URLs with NO host validation (case "sitemap", lines 726-731 store val verbatim). CrawlEndpoints (154) feeds robotsResult.sitemapURLs into fromSitemap (158). fromSitemap line 789 calls c.fetchBody(ctx, u, ...) on every queued URL — including child <sitemap><loc> entries (queued 796, parsed 848-851) — BEFORE any host check. fetchBody (1020-1042) does c.client.Do(req) on the crawler client with no CheckRedirect. The host filter at lines 807-815 runs only AFTER the fetch and only decides which discovered <loc> PAGE endpoints to KEEP, not which sitemap docs are FETCHED. So a target that serves `Sitemap: http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/...` (or a 302 to it) gets that URL fetched by the scanner. The fromJS resolveURL (484) and HTML-link paths corroborate the broader pattern.

4) Not an accepted tradeoff — the opposite. docs/threat-model.md "Active scanner safety envelope" explicitly promises envelope #4 ("No automatic crawl beyond same-host ... Fendix does not 'discover' external hosts and start scanning them") and #3 ("Fendix cannot be hijacked into being a scan-launcher for an attacker who controls the spec or wordlist"), and states "A break of any of these is a security vulnerability in Fendix." The code breaks #4 directly. Neither threat-model.md nor SECURITY.md documents any private-IP/metadata SSRF mitigation or a "trusted-target-only" carve-out for discovery.

Severity remains high, not critical: exploitation requires the operator to point Fendix at an attacker-influenced/untrusted target (or run it as the hosted GH App / `fendix serve` multi-tenant service the roadmap implies). For the common "scan my own asset with authorization" CLI use, the operator already controls the target, so impact is bounded — which is why this is high, not critical. But the multi-tenant/hosted path and the "scan an untrusted third-party URL" path both yield genuine SSRF to 169.254.169.254 / internal services and potential cloud-credential theft.
surviving.falsePositiveRisk: In the dominant single-operator CLI workflow the operator must already be authorized to scan the target they choose, so a self-targeted scan is not a meaningful pivot — the SSRF only becomes a real cross-trust-boundary issue when the scanned target is attacker-influenced or when Fendix runs as a hosted/multi-tenant service (GH App / `fendix serve`), which is roadmap rather than shipped. The redirect-following (default 10) is also standard Go http.Client behavior, not a Fendix-specific bug, though combined with no IP filtering it widens the surface. None of this refutes the finding (the same-host guarantee in the threat model is broken regardless), but it bounds real-world impact to deployments that scan untrusted targets.

surviving.title: Plugin runner follows symlinked plugin dirs and execs entrypoint with no ownership/permission check (symlink + world-writable trust)
surviving.description: Discover os.Stat's each entry specifically to follow symlinks into plugin directories (comment lines 189-193) and then Run execs `filepath.Join(p.Dir, p.Entrypoint)` directly (line 302) with no check on file ownership or that the directory / entrypoint is not world-writable, group-writable, or a symlink to somewhere outside the plugins root. The repo-local root `.fendix/plugins/` (DefaultRoots, line 432) is inside the scanned repository — for the GH App / CI flows that clone an untrusted PR and scan it, a PR can add `.fendix/plugins/evil/plugin.yaml` + an executable entrypoint, and a subsequent scan that runs plugins would execute attacker code. Even outside CI, a symlink in the plugins dir can redirect the entrypoint to an arbitrary on-disk executable. validate() (lines 253-283) blocks `..` and absolute entrypoints but a symlinked entrypoint or symlinked plugin dir bypasses that intent.
surviving.impact: Code execution as the scanning user from a repo-local plugin planted by an untrusted PR, or from a symlink/world-writable plugin directory on a shared host. The token-redaction in redactPluginEnv reduces credential exposure but does not prevent arbitrary code execution.
surviving.recommendation: Do not auto-discover repo-local plugins when scanning untrusted code (or require an explicit opt-in flag / allowlist). Before exec, lstat the resolved entrypoint and reject if it is a symlink escaping the plugins root, if the file or any parent dir is writable by group/other, or if the owner differs from the current user. Consider refusing to follow symlinked plugin directories entirely.
surviving.verifierReasoning:
Code matches the finding exactly. Discover (go/internal/plugin/plugin.go:187-216) does `info, err := os.Stat(dir)` at line 194 specifically to follow symlinks into plugin dirs (comment lines 189-193 confirms intent: "Stat the entry so symlinked plugin dirs ... discover too"). loadPlugin->validate (lines 253-283) only blocks an absolute or `..`-containing Entrypoint string; it performs zero checks on file ownership, group/world-writability, or whether Dir/Entrypoint is a symlink to outside the plugins root. Run (lines 294-310) then execs `exec.CommandContext(runCtx, filepath.Join(p.Dir, p.Entrypoint))` with `cmd.Dir = p.Dir` directly — arbitrary executable, no trust check.

The repo-local root is real: DefaultRoots (line 429-438) returns `filepath.Join(cwd, ".fendix", "plugins")` first, and runPlugins (orchestrator.go:570-573) uses `cwd, _ := os.Getwd()`. Plugins run by default — orchestrator.go:352 gates only on `!o.cfg.NoPlugins` (default false, --no-plugins to disable). Whitebox/hybrid plugins fire whenever --code/--spec is set (orchestrator.go:583,587-603).

Exploitability via the SHIPPED reference CI workflow is confirmed: examples/github-actions/fendix-scan.yml triggers `on: pull_request` (line 37), does `actions/checkout@v4` (line 51), then `fendix scan --code ./` (lines 95-96) run from the workspace, so os.Getwd() == checked-out PR head. A fork PR that adds `.fendix/plugins/evil/plugin.yaml` (mode: whitebox) + an executable entrypoint is discovered by Discover and executed on the CI runner — classic poisoned-pipeline RCE. This path is NOT covered by the threat model: docs/threat-model.md explicitly excludes "threats from a malicious target to Fendix" (lines 42-45) and never mentions plugins; plugins.md "Security model" (lines 494-520) frames plugin install as a deliberate operator act ("Treat plugin installation the same as installing any other binary") and never contemplates a plugin arriving inside the scanned repo. So this is an unaddressed gap, not an accepted tradeoff.

The symlink sub-claim is also confirmed and the docs are demonstrably stale/wrong about it: plugins.md lines 391-395 and 418 claim "The discovery walk treats symlinks as regular files and skips them," but the code (the os.Stat follow at line 194, added under TASK-130) does the opposite and intentionally follows symlinked plugin dirs — so a symlinked dir/entrypoint bypasses the spirit of validate()'s path checks.

Severity raised to high: unauthenticated arbitrary code execution on the scanning host/CI runner from untrusted PR content, reachable through a default-on feature and the project's own recommended CI integration. Not the highest (critical) because it requires the operator to have plugins present in the repo-local root path and to run the default-plugins, pull_request-triggered workflow; a hardened operator can pass --no-plugins or use pull_request_target gating.
surviving.falsePositiveRisk: The finding's specific "GH App" framing is partly inaccurate: in go/internal/ghapp/scanner.go (lines 125-130) the scan is `exec.CommandContext(ctx, fendixBin, "scan", "--code", dir, ...)` and scanCmd.Dir is never set, so the fendix-app process's cwd (under os.TempDir clone is separate, and the K8s manifest uses readOnlyRootFilesystem) — NOT the cloned untrusted repo — is what DefaultRoots(cwd) resolves the repo-local plugin root from. So the precise GH App attack as described does not plant plugins from the PR. However, the finding also explicitly names "CI flows," and the shipped reference GitHub Actions workflow IS vulnerable because it runs `fendix scan --code ./` from the checked-out repo cwd. The world-writable/symlink-to-outside angle is a weaker, shared-host local concern; the PR-plant RCE via the reference CI workflow is the load-bearing, confirmed vector. Net: the core supply-chain RCE claim holds; only the GH-App-specific detail is overstated.

surviving.title: Installation token embedded in git remote URL leaks via process args and .git/config
surviving.description: FendixScanner.Run() builds an authenticated clone URL via injectInstallationToken (u.User = url.UserPassword("x-access-token", token)) and then passes that full URL — token included — as a literal argv element to `git remote add origin <authedURL>` (steps slice line 107). git then persists that URL, token and all, into the on-disk .git/config of the temp clone. The token is therefore exposed in two cleartext sinks: (1) the process argument list, readable by any other local user/process via `ps auxww`, /proc/<pid>/cmdline, or container introspection for the lifetime of the git process; and (2) <tmpdir>/fendix-scan-*/.git/config on disk. The on-disk copy is removed by `defer os.RemoveAll(dir)` only at the end of Run(), and the fendix subprocess (which can be arbitrary code paths under scan) runs with --code pointed at that same dir while the token-bearing .git/config still exists.
surviving.impact: A co-located process/user on the webhook host (multi-tenant CI runner, sidecar, compromised dependency in the fendix scan subprocess) can read a live GitHub App installation token (1-hour validity, write scope to the installation's repos). This is privilege escalation to repo write/PR/Code-Scanning access for every repo in the installation.
surviving.recommendation: Do not put the token in the URL/argv. Use `git -c http.extraheader="Authorization: Basic <base64(x-access-token:token)>"` passed via stdin config, or set GIT_ASKPASS / a credential helper that feeds the token over a pipe, or use the `credential.helper` with an env var. At minimum, write the remote with a placeholder and inject the credential out-of-band, and ensure the token never reaches .git/config. Also scope the temp dir to 0700 and avoid the fendix subprocess being able to read .git (it already skips .git in the secrets walk, but other paths may not).
surviving.verifierReasoning: All cited code is accurate. In /Users/asaied/WorkDir/Fendix/fendix-engine/go/internal/ghapp/scanner.go: injectInstallationToken (lines 166-176) sets u.User = url.UserPassword("x-access-token", token) and returns u.String(); Run() (line 100) builds authedURL from it and at line 107 places that token-bearing URL as a literal argv element {gitBin, "-C", dir, "remote", "add", "origin", authedURL}, passed to exec.CommandContext via runCommand (lines 112-116, 178-186). I reproduced both sinks locally: (1) `git remote add origin https://x-access-token:<token>@github.com/...` writes the token verbatim into .git/config (url = https://x-access-token:ghs_...@github.com/owner/repo.git), and (2) the URL is a real process argument, exposed via ps/`/proc/<pid>/cmdline` for the git process lifetime. The token comes from h.Tokens.Get (handler.go:176) — a real GitHub App installation token (auth.go InstallationToken{Token, ExpiresAt}, ~1h validity, installation-scoped write access). Crucially, fendix scan runs with --code <dir> (scanner.go:125-130) against the SAME dir that still holds .git/config; defer os.RemoveAll(dir) (line 98) only fires when Run() returns, so the on-disk token persists for the entire scan of untrusted repo contents — matching the cited compromised-dependency vector. No git credential helper / GIT_ASKPASS / core.askPass / -c http.extraHeader mitigation is used; redactToken only scrubs error strings (line 114), not the live argv or config. The project threat-model (docs/threat-model.md) covers only the active target scanner, not the GitHub App webhook token handling; its T3 stance ("No credential storage... nothing persists to disk") is contradicted by this behavior rather than endorsing it. So this is not a documented/accepted tradeoff. Embedding credentials in a git remote URL is a well-known anti-pattern (git docs and GitHub guidance warn against it). Severity remains high: the leaked secret grants write/PR/code-scanning access to every repo in the installation, with realistic local/co-located and same-UID adversaries.
surviving.falsePositiveRisk: One mitigating fact tempers the "any local user via ps/disk" framing: os.MkdirTemp creates the temp dir with mode 0700 (verified: drwx------), so a DIFFERENT local UID cannot traverse in to read .git/config on disk — the cross-user on-disk vector is partially closed. However, the process-args vector (ps auxww / /proc/<pid>/cmdline) is world-readable by default on Linux and is NOT mitigated, and the same-UID on-disk vector (the fendix scan subprocess / a compromised dependency in the scanned code, root, or a container sharing the mount namespace) is fully open. The token is also short-lived (max ~1h) and only installation-scoped, not org-admin, so blast radius is bounded to the installation's repos and the token's declared permissions. These reduce but do not eliminate exploitability; high (not critical) is the appropriate adjusted severity.

surviving.title: Unbounded recursion in taint tracer lets one crafted file suppress all injection findings
surviving.description: _trace_to_source() recurses through scope assignments with only a cycle guard (the `visited` frozenset) and NO depth limit. A single function body containing a long linear assignment chain (a1=a0; a2=a1; ...; sink(aN)) drives Python recursion past sys.getrecursionlimit and raises RecursionError. The visitor call `visitor.visit(tree)` at line 113 is OUTSIDE the parse try/except (which only catches OSError/SyntaxError at line 109), so RecursionError propagates out of _analyze_python -> out of ASTAnalyzer.run()'s os.walk loop (lines 85-94) -> and is only caught by engine._run_check's broad `except Exception`. The os.walk is abandoned: every file not yet visited is silently skipped. Reproduced: a ~4000-line bomb file named to sort first causes a co-located file with a real `os.system(request.args.get('cmd'))` to NEVER be analyzed.
surviving.impact: Finding-suppression / denial-of-analysis. In the enterprise PR-scanning use case, an attacker opening a malicious PR can include one innocuous-looking 'bomb' source file alongside their real injection/SQLi/SSRF vulnerability; the bomb aborts the entire injection pass and the real vuln is reported as zero findings — fendix gives a clean bill of health. The Go side (orchestrator.runWhiteboxScan) treats the returned partial/empty findings as authoritative.
surviving.recommendation: Wrap the per-file `visitor.visit(tree)` (line 113) in its own try/except that catches Exception (including RecursionError) and logs+continues to the next file, so one file can never abort the whole walk. Independently, add a depth/hop cap to _trace_to_source (e.g. bound recursion to ~50 hops via a counter param) and cap taint_chain length so a long chain also can't blow past readFindings' 1MiB line limit on the Go side.
surviving.verifierReasoning:
Every load-bearing claim verified against the actual code and reproduced end-to-end.

1) Unbounded recursion, no depth limit: `_trace_to_source` (ast_analyzer.py:274-300) recurses one level per assignment link — `deeper = self._trace_to_source(assigned, visited | {n.id})`. The `visited` frozenset only guards assignment CYCLES (a=b;b=a), not linear chains (a1=a0; a2=a1; ...). There is no depth counter, no sys.setrecursionlimit anywhere in python/ (grep confirmed). A linear chain of N assignments drives N levels of Python recursion.

2) Exception escapes the parse guard: `_analyze_python` wraps only `filepath.stat()/read_text()/ast.parse()` in `try ... except (OSError, SyntaxError)` (lines 104-110). The `visitor.visit(tree)` at line 113 is OUTSIDE that block. RecursionError subclasses RuntimeError -> Exception, so it propagates out of _analyze_python and out of run()'s os.walk loop (lines 85-94).

3) Whole-pass abandonment: engine.py:34 `_run_check` wraps the entire `ASTAnalyzer(...).run(...)` (the whole os.walk) in one `except Exception`. So one file's RecursionError aborts the entire injection pass; every file not yet walked is silently skipped, then the engine prints `{"done": true, "total": counter}` and exits 0.

Reproduced: a ~16KB file (chain of ~1000 assignments, well under the 1MB _MAX_FILE_BYTES cap at line 24) raises RecursionError at the default limit of 1000. Running the real engine.py via stdin/stdout on a dir containing the bomb plus a second file with `os.system(request.args.get('cmd'))` produced: stderr "check 'injection (ast)' failed: maximum recursion depth exceeded", stdout `{"done": true, "total": 0}`, exit code 0. The real command-injection vuln was never reported.

4) Go treats partial/empty as authoritative: plugin.go readPluginFindings (368-409) returns no error when the done line carries no `error` field; cmd.Wait() returns nil for exit 0. The GitHub App scanner (ghapp/scanner.go) runs `fendix scan` against an untrusted PR checkout (`git checkout FETCH_HEAD`) and only treats a non-zero exit as failure — so the empty findings are posted as a clean PR comment. The threat-model.md does not document this denial-of-analysis vector.

This is a real finding-suppression / denial-of-analysis bug exploitable by anyone who can place a file in the scanned tree (the documented enterprise PR-scanning use case).
surviving.falsePositiveRisk: Scope is narrower than a total scan blackout: only the Python AST injection pass is aborted. The Go-native secrets and semgrep scanners and the Python deps check run in separate _run_check calls / separate Go code paths and are unaffected, so they would still report. Also, the victim file is only skipped if it is walked AFTER the bomb file; os.walk yields filenames in unsorted os.scandir order, so an attacker wanting to suppress a SPECIFIC pre-existing file must control walk ordering (e.g. place the bomb in the repo root, which a top-down walk visits before subdirectory files, or name it to scan first). In practice the attacker controls the PR contents and can satisfy this easily, and any bomb reliably suppresses all not-yet-walked files. Severity stays high (not critical) because it suppresses one analyzer family rather than the whole scan, and requires the attacker to be able to add a file to the analyzed tree.

surviving.title: README "Zero outbound" trust claim for code scans is false — dep scanners call osv.dev / vuln.go.dev by default
surviving.description: README trust table: `fendix scan --code ...` -> "Zero outbound. Reads source from disk." plus "If a future release adds anything that talks to a non-target host, it'll be opt-in, documented... That's the contract." But orchestrator.go:206-273 runs three native dep-CVE scanners on every --code scan by default (NoNativeDeps defaults false): pip -> https://api.osv.dev (deps/pip/scanner.go:81, client.Do :444/:754), npm -> osv.dev (deps/npm/scanner.go:310/510), govulncheck -> https://vuln.go.dev (deps/govulncheck/scanner.go via golang.org/x/vuln).
surviving.impact: Enterprises evaluate Fendix on this trust statement. A regulated/air-gapped customer running `fendix scan --code` believing it is hermetic silently exfiltrates their dependency list (package names + pinned versions) to api.osv.dev and vuln.go.dev — a compliance violation and a contradiction of an explicitly stated contract.
surviving.recommendation: Update the README trust table to disclose --code scans query osv.dev / vuln.go.dev for dep CVEs unless --no-native-deps/--offline is set (naming hosts), OR make dep-CVE network lookups opt-in. Wire --offline so code scans can be genuinely hermetic; reconcile with docs/threat-model.md.
surviving.verifierReasoning: All claimed facts verified against current source. (1) README trust table at README.md:22 states `fendix scan --code ...` -> "Zero outbound. Reads source from disk." and README.md:26 states the contract: "If a future release adds anything that talks to a non-target host, it'll be opt-in, documented in this section, and named in the CHANGELOG. That's the contract." README.md:187 reinforces "Analyze source code without making any network requests." (2) orchestrator.go:206 gates the native dep-CVE scanners on `if o.cfg.CodePath != "" && !o.cfg.NoNativeDeps`, then unconditionally runs govulncheck.Scan (:207), pip.ScanRecursiveWithOptions (:231), and npm.Scan (:247). (3) The default is ON: main.go:392 registers `flags.Bool("no-native-deps", false, ...)`, so NoNativeDeps defaults false and the dep scanners fire on every --code scan with no opt-in. (4) The outbound endpoints are real, hardcoded production defaults pointing at non-target third-party hosts: pip/scanner.go:81 `var osvAPIBase = "https://api.osv.dev"` with POSTs at :439 (/v1/querybatch) and :749 (/v1/query); npm/scanner.go:67 same `var osvAPIBase = "https://api.osv.dev"` with POSTs at :305 and :505; govulncheck/scanner.go:46 documents the DB default of https://vuln.go.dev, invoked via scan.Command (golang.org/x/vuln). These POST the dependency list (package names + pinned versions) to api.osv.dev / vuln.go.dev. This is a non-target host, sent by default, with no documentation in the trust section — a direct contradiction of both the trust table and the explicitly stated "opt-in, documented... contract." The README even contradicts itself internally: line 187 says "without making any network requests" while line 193 says the same scan "runs ... dependency CVE scanning," which is the network-calling component. Severity high is justified: enterprises explicitly evaluate Fendix on this trust statement, and an air-gapped/regulated customer running `fendix scan --code` believing it hermetic would silently transmit their dependency inventory to two external services, a real compliance and contract violation.
surviving.falsePositiveRisk: The outbound calls only fire when the relevant ecosystem manifest exists: govulncheck returns ErrNoGoMod when no go.mod is present (scanner.go:58-60), pip needs a requirements/pyproject manifest under the path, and npm needs package-lock.json (else ErrNoLockfile / advisory). So a --code scan of a pure-text or manifest-less directory would in fact make zero outbound calls, and a network-down environment degrades to slog.Warn-and-continue rather than failing. Additionally, `--no-native-deps` exists as an escape hatch. However, real-world repos overwhelmingly contain such manifests (that is the primary target of a dep-CVE scan), the README makes an unqualified absolute "Zero outbound" claim with no caveat, and the opt-out is undocumented in the trust section — so the docs-vs-reality contradiction stands for the common case.

surviving.title: GitHub App runs a 15-minute clone+scan synchronously inside the webhook HTTP handler with no concurrency limit
surviving.description: HandlePullRequest/HandleCheckRun call runScan() synchronously inside ServeHTTP's dispatch (webhook.go:149). runScan clones and shells out to `fendix scan` with a 15-min timeout (handler.go:16,140); the HTTP 200 (webhook.go:155) only returns after the scan finishes. Server WriteTimeout is 60s (cmd/fendix-app/main.go:75); GitHub's webhook delivery timeout is ~10s. No semaphore/queue/in-flight cap exists in ghapp; fly.toml runs min_machines_running=1, hard_limit=100.
surviving.impact: (1) Every real scan blows past WriteTimeout/GitHub's delivery timeout, so GitHub marks delivery failed and redelivers — duplicate concurrent scans; repeated timeouts cause GitHub to auto-disable the webhook. (2) No concurrency cap means N open PRs spawn N simultaneous clone+scan subprocesses on one machine, exhausting CPU/memory/disk (resource-exhaustion DoS). Unfit for multi-repo enterprise installs as written.
surviving.recommendation: Acknowledge the webhook immediately (200/202 after signature verify + decode), run scans on a bounded background worker pool with a concurrency semaphore + queue, dedupe by X-GitHub-Delivery / (repo,headSHA), and report via the Checks API. Document max concurrent scans + machine sizing in docs/github-app.md.
surviving.verifierReasoning: All cited code verified as described. (1) Synchronous execution: webhook.go ServeHTTP calls s.dispatch(ctx, body) at line 149 and only reaches w.WriteHeader(http.StatusOK) at line 155 AFTER dispatch returns. dispatch routes pull_request/check_run to HandlePullRequest/HandleCheckRun (webhook.go:165-170), which call `return h.runScan(bgCtx, ctx, scanInputs{...})` directly (handler.go:143, 298). runScan synchronously acquires a token, calls scanner.Run, posts the comment, and uploads SARIF before returning. So the HTTP 200 is emitted only after the full clone+scan completes. (2) Timeout: HandlerScanTimeout = 15 * time.Minute (handler.go:16), applied via context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), HandlerScanTimeout) (handler.go:140, 295). Notably it derives from context.Background(), not the request context, so an HTTP client/server timeout will NOT cancel the in-flight scan — it runs to its own 15-min cap. (3) scanner.go confirms the work is heavy: shells out to git init/remote/fetch/checkout then `fendix scan` (Semgrep) and `fendix report` via exec.CommandContext, with a per-scan temp dir. (4) main.go:75 WriteTimeout: 60 * time.Second — any scan over 60s wall-clock will have its response write killed by the server, and GitHub's webhook delivery timeout (~10s) is far exceeded by any real scan, so GitHub marks the delivery failed and redelivers; persistent failures trigger GitHub's webhook auto-disable. Redelivery against the same head SHA produces duplicate concurrent scans. (5) Concurrency: grep over internal/ghapp shows NO semaphore/errgroup/limiter/in-flight counter; the only sync.Mutex (auth.go:199) and goroutine (auth.go:245) belong to the token-cache single-flight, unrelated to scan concurrency. net/http handles each delivery in its own goroutine, unbounded. (6) fly.toml confirms min_machines_running=1 (line 27), hard_limit=100 (line 31), a single shared-cpu-2x / 1024mb VM (lines 41-43). N concurrent PR webhooks => N concurrent git fetch + Semgrep subprocesses on one 2-vCPU/1GB machine => CPU/memory/disk exhaustion (OOM/thrash), a real resource-exhaustion DoS. Additionally, the fly.toml comment (lines 48-51) asserts "The webhook handler responds 200 immediately and processes async ... clone+scan is goroutine-local" — this is directly contradicted by the handler code, confirming the synchronous behavior is an oversight, not an intentional design. No guard, validation, or documented threat-model tradeoff mitigates this. The finding is accurate and exploitable under normal enterprise PR volume.
surviving.falsePositiveRisk: The /webhook endpoint is gated by HMAC-SHA256 signature verification (webhook.go:129), so the trigger is authenticated GitHub deliveries, not arbitrary unauthenticated attackers — the DoS arises from legitimate PR/scan volume plus GitHub's own redelivery loop, not an external attack vector. The body-size cap (MaxWebhookBodyBytes, 4 MiB) limits payload memory but does nothing for clone/scan resource use. For a small single-repo install with infrequent PRs and fast-completing scans (<60s), the WriteTimeout and concurrency issues may never manifest, which is why this is high rather than critical. The 15-min cap also bounds per-scan goroutine lifetime, preventing unbounded-duration hangs (but not concurrent resource exhaustion).

surviving.title: install.sh curl|sh path has no signature verification and fetches checksum from the same origin as the binary
surviving.description: The canonical install path advertised everywhere (curl -fsSL https://get.fendix.dev/install.sh | sh) downloads the binary from GitHub releases (line 74) and, for integrity, downloads ${URL}.sha256 from the *same* base URL (line 86-87) and compares (line 99). The .sig/.crt cosign sidecars that release.yml produces and that SECURITY.md spends ~90 lines documenting are never fetched or verified by install.sh — grep for cosign/gpg/verify/.sig/.crt in install.sh returns nothing. A self-fetched checksum provides only corruption detection, not authenticity: an attacker who can tamper with the release asset (compromised mirror repo, MITM if get.fendix.dev/CDN is breached, or a malicious mirror push) simply serves a matching .sha256 alongside the swapped binary and the check passes.
surviving.impact: The most common install path for an end-user security tool ships with no supply-chain integrity. SECURITY.md (lines 98-201) explicitly claims 'every release binary ... signed with cosign keyless' and tells operators to verify — but the default installer does not, so users get a false sense of assurance. A compromised get.fendix.dev or homebrew-fendix mirror leads to silent RCE on every machine that runs the one-liner, including CI runners (benchmark.yml:53-55 pipes this exact one-liner into sh).
surviving.recommendation: Make install.sh fetch the .sig + .crt sidecars and run `cosign verify-blob` (or at minimum verify a detached minisign/GPG signature whose public key is baked into the script), failing closed when verification tooling or signatures are absent. Until then, stop advertising cosign verification as the security story for the default install path, and pin the checksum source to a different trust domain than the binary.
surviving.verifierReasoning: All cited code verified in /Users/asaied/WorkDir/Fendix/fendix-engine/scripts/install.sh. Line 74 downloads the binary from github.com/${REPO}/releases/download/${VERSION}/${BINARY}; lines 86-87 fetch ${URL}.sha256 from the same base URL; lines 89-101 compute and compare only the SHA-256. A grep of install.sh for cosign/gpg/.sig/.crt/keyless/attest returns nothing (only the checksum 'Verifying...' string and the verify() install-check function). So the installer performs no authenticity verification — exactly as claimed. The supporting claims also check out: release.yml lines 126-175 produce ${BINARY}.sig and ${BINARY}.crt via `cosign sign-blob` keyless, and the enforce-signing job (lines 22-37) refuses to release a v* tag unless COSIGN_ENABLED is set, so v0.6.0+ releases DO carry the sidecars install.sh ignores. SECURITY.md lines 98-201 document ~100 lines of cosign verify-blob / verify-attestation instructions and line 100-101 claim 'every release binary ... signed with cosign'. benchmark.yml line 53 pipes `curl -fsSL https://get.fendix.dev/install.sh | ... sh` directly into CI runners. The core security critique is sound: a checksum fetched from the same origin as the binary provides only transit/corruption integrity, not authenticity — an actor who can alter the release asset can alter the matching .sha256, and the installer never consults the cosign material the project goes to great lengths to produce and document. This is the canonical, advertised install path and it auto-runs on CI runners, so the gap is real and reachable. I downgrade from high to medium for exploitability/altitude reasons: (1) the binary is pulled directly from github.com release-download URLs over HTTPS, not from get.fendix.dev or an arbitrary CDN (get.fendix.dev only serves install.sh itself), so a passive network MITM is not realistic against GitHub TLS — the realistic exploit requires compromising the homebrew-fendix release assets or the get.fendix.dev origin, and either of those compromises (especially a tampered install.sh served from get.fendix.dev) would also defeat any in-script verification, blunting the marginal protection cosign-in-installer would add against the strongest attacker; (2) checksum-from-same-origin is the prevailing pattern for curl|sh installers industry-wide, and SECURITY.md lines 194-195 explicitly acknowledge the installer lacks a 'cosign-verified upgrade path' and recommend pinning a tag, so it is a partially-documented known gap rather than a silent false claim. It still warrants medium because the doc's blanket 'every release binary is signed' messaging plus an unverifying default installer creates the false-assurance condition the finding describes, and hardening the installer to verify cosign signatures (or at minimum pin and verify against a baked-in key/identity) is a clear, achievable improvement for a security product.
surviving.falsePositiveRisk: Could be argued down to low/accepted-tradeoff because: the binary transits GitHub HTTPS (not an attacker-controllable plaintext channel), making passive MITM infeasible; the same-origin-checksum pattern is near-universal for shell installers; and SECURITY.md already flags the installer gap and recommends tag-pinning/manual cosign verification. An attacker capable of the cited compromises (release-asset tamper or get.fendix.dev breach) is largely also capable of serving a modified install.sh, which would bypass any in-script verification — so the residual risk reduced by fixing only the installer is smaller than the 'silent RCE on every machine' framing implies.

surviving.title: Checksum verification is silently skipped when sha256sum/shasum are absent
surviving.description: When neither sha256sum nor shasum is on PATH, the script warns and sets ACTUAL="$EXPECTED" (lines 94-96), guaranteeing the equality check at line 99 passes. The whole `if curl ... .sha256` block (line 87) is also only entered `2>/dev/null` best-effort — if the checksum download fails, verification is skipped entirely with no warning. So the only integrity control degrades to a no-op on minimal images (many slim containers lack both tools) without aborting the install.
surviving.impact: On minimal/CI environments the binary is installed and chmod +x'd with zero integrity checking, and the user sees a green success message. Combined with the no-signature finding, the integrity guarantee is best-effort at best and silently absent at worst.
surviving.recommendation: Fail closed: if a checksum is published but no hashing tool is available, error out rather than assuming a match. Treat a missing/failed checksum download as a hard error for non-interactive installs, or require the signature path instead.
surviving.verifierReasoning:
The cited code exists exactly as described in /Users/asaied/WorkDir/Fendix/fendix-engine/scripts/install.sh. Lines 90-97: when neither sha256sum nor shasum is on PATH, the else branch (lines 94-96) prints `warn "No sha256sum or shasum found — skipping checksum verification"` and sets `ACTUAL="$EXPECTED"`, which deterministically makes the equality check at line 99 (`if [ "$EXPECTED" != "$ACTUAL" ]`) pass. This is a fail-open degradation of the only automatic integrity control. Separately, the entire verification block at line 87 is gated on `curl -fsSL -o ... "$CHECKSUM_URL" 2>/dev/null` succeeding, with no `else`, so if the .sha256 sidecar download fails the verification is skipped silently with no warning. Both sub-claims are real; no guard handles them.

Critically, the installer performs NO signature verification: grep confirms zero cosign/.sig/verify-blob references in install.sh. The release pipeline (.github/workflows/release.yml) does cosign-sign binaries and produces .sig/.crt artifacts, and docs/install.md advertises "signature-verified" installs, but cosign verification is purely a manual step the user must run themselves — the advertised `curl -fsSL https://get.fendix.dev/install.sh | sh` one-liner never fetches or checks the signature. So the sha256 sidecar comparison is genuinely the sole automatic integrity gate in the default install path, and it degrades to a no-op on minimal images lacking coreutils/perl-less busybox-style environments. After verification turns into a no-op, line 104 chmod +x's the binary and line 131 prints a green "✓ fendix installed successfully!" banner — a deceptive success signal. The preconditions (slim/distroless/Alpine-ish CI containers lacking both tools) are realistic, not hypothetical.

Severity held at medium rather than raised: even when the checksum check works, it is fetched over the same TLS/CDN channel as the binary, so it only defends against accidental corruption and same-origin partial tampering — a full GitHub-release/CDN compromise would serve a matching forged checksum anyway. Exploitation of the fail-open path also still requires an attacker to be positioned to substitute the binary in transit (HTTPS-protected) or compromise the release host. So this is a real fail-open weakening of a modest-value control plus a misleading success UX, which is solidly medium, not high.
surviving.falsePositiveRisk: The .sha256 sidecar files are reliably generated and uploaded by release.yml (lines 89, 718 upload glob), so the line-87 "download fails silently" path is an edge case (transient/asymmetric failure where the binary downloads but the sidecar does not) rather than a routine occurrence — that specific sub-claim is weaker. The missing-tool path is the load-bearing one: it could be argued as a low/accepted tradeoff since most real Linux/macOS hosts ship coreutils (sha256sum) or BSD shasum, making truly toolless environments a minority. The control's intrinsic value is also limited because checksum and binary share the same trust channel, so a determined supply-chain attacker is not stopped by it even when it functions. These factors cap the realistic impact at medium and explain why a reviewer could reasonably downgrade toward low for a non-internet-facing enterprise deployment that installs from trusted internal mirrors.

surviving.title: Release-critical tools (nfpm, syft, actionlint) installed via `go install ...@vX` mutable tags, bypassing the repo's own SHA-pin policy
surviving.description: The repo enforces a strict 40-char-SHA pin policy for `uses:` actions (ci.yml:93-100 actively fails CI on any floating @vN). But the release pipeline installs three third-party tools that directly touch shipped artifacts via `go install <module>@vN`: nfpm v2.40.0 (builds the .deb/.rpm users install, release.yml:99), syft v1.18.1 (generates the SBOMs that procurement trusts, release.yml:192 and 470), and actionlint v1.7.4 (ci.yml:83). These are semver *tags*, which are mutable on the upstream VCS; none are in go/go.sum (confirmed via grep), so they get no go.sum pre-pinning — go install resolves the tag and TOFU-verifies against sum.golang.org at install time. The workflow comments even acknowledge this ('The version is pinned; dependabot will bump it', release.yml:189-192) but a version *tag* is weaker than a module pseudo-version+hash and far weaker than the SHA pins demanded elsewhere.
surviving.impact: An upstream tag-move or account compromise on goreleaser/nfpm or anchore/syft would let an attacker inject code into the exact tools that produce the signed .deb/.rpm and the SBOMs — the artifacts and provenance metadata that the cosign/SLSA story is built on. This is the precise gap (third-party build tooling not SHA/hash-pinned) the SHA-pin policy was meant to close, applied inconsistently. The SHA-pin guard (ci.yml:96) only greps `uses:` lines, so it does not catch these `go install` lines.
surviving.recommendation: Pin these tools to module pseudo-versions or vendor them with go.sum entries (a dedicated tools.go/`go.mod` tool directive), or install from SHA-pinned release artifacts with checksum verification. Extend the ci.yml SHA-pin guard to also flag `go install ...@vN` in workflow files so the policy actually covers build tooling.
surviving.verifierReasoning: Every checkable claim holds against the actual code. (1) The SHA-pin guard at ci.yml:93-100 greps ONLY `uses:` lines (regex `uses: [a-zA-Z0-9_./-]+@v[0-9]+\b`) and exits 1 on a floating @vN — it cannot and does not catch `go install` lines in `run:` blocks. Confirmed by reading the step. (2) The three tools are installed via mutable semver tags exactly as cited: nfpm@v2.40.0 (release.yml:99, builds the shipped .deb/.rpm), syft@v1.18.1 (release.yml:192 and 470, generates the signed/shipped SBOMs), actionlint@v1.7.4 (ci.yml:83). (3) grep of go/go.mod and go/go.sum for goreleaser/nfpm/anchore/syft/rhysd/actionlint returns nothing; there is no `tool` directive and no tools.go in the main module — so these get no committed-hash pre-pinning. (4) The threat-model T6 (docs/threat-model.md:201-228) frames the SHA-pin mitigation explicitly around third-party *actions* (`uses:` lines) and claims "No third-party CI actions in critical path" — it never asserts go install tools are hash-pinned, so this is a genuine gap between the advertised policy and the release-tool reality, applied inconsistently to the exact tooling (nfpm, syft) that produces signed artifacts and provenance. (5) Notably the workflow comment at release.yml:189-190 ("The version is pinned; dependabot will bump it") is materially inaccurate: .github/dependabot.yml watches only `github-actions` (which parses `uses:` lines, not shell `go install` strings) and `gomod` scoped to /go/go.mod (where these tools do not appear) — so dependabot will NOT bump these versions. The finding is real and well-grounded. I downgrade from high to medium on exploitability grounds the finding overstates: `go install module@v2.40.0` on a fresh CI runner is verified against the Go checksum database (GOSUMDB=sum.golang.org), whose transparency-log hash for an already-published version is immutable — so a retroactive upstream *tag-move* (the primary scenario the finding emphasizes) would cause a checksum mismatch and FAIL the build, not silently inject code. The finding's phrase "TOFU-verifies against sum.golang.org at install time" is wrong for an already-seen version. The genuine residual risk is narrower: a brand-new malicious release pushed under a compromised goreleaser/anchore/rhysd account, which sum.golang.org would faithfully record — but this same caveat applies to any dependency and is the same class of gap that SHA-pinning leaves open before a new SHA is recorded. Impact-if-exploited on nfpm/syft is high (touches signed packages and SBOMs), but the precondition is specific upstream-publisher compromise and the SBOM tampering would still surface under a valid Actions identity rather than breaking signatures; actionlint touches no shipped artifact at all and inflates the finding. Net: a true, accurate supply-chain hygiene inconsistency with a misleading code comment, but medium rather than high given the checksum-DB mitigation against tag-moves and the narrow compromise precondition.
surviving.falsePositiveRisk: Not a false positive — the code, the guard scope, the absent go.sum entries, and the inaccurate dependabot comment are all directly verified. The main reason a reviewer might rate it lower than reported is the Go checksum database (sum.golang.org), which already protects against the tag-move scenario the finding leans on; some orgs set GOFLAGS=-mod=mod or GONOSUMDB and would lose even that, but this repo shows no such override. Treat as a defensible hardening recommendation (pin via go.mod `tool` directive + go.sum, or add these to the SHA-pin guard), not a live remote-exploitable vuln.

surviving.title: Untrusted fork-PR code is cloned and scanned while a write-scoped installation token is live in the process
surviving.description: On pull_request opened/synchronize/reopened the handler acquires an installation token (handler.go:176, scopes per app/manifest.yml:36-46 include security_events:write, checks:write, pull_requests:write) and then clones the PR head and runs `fendix scan --code <dir>` over attacker-authored source (scanner.go:125-133). fendix scan parses untrusted code (Python AST analyzer, semgrep, dep manifests) inside the same process tree that holds the write-scoped token. The CloneURL is taken from p.PullRequest.Head.Repo.CloneURL (handler.go:135) which for a fork PR is the attacker's fork. There is no isolation/sandbox documented around the scan (no seccomp/no-network mentioned for the scan subprocess), and the token sits in the clone URL and in the TokenSource cache (auth.go:226-272) for up to an hour. This is the GitHub-Actions `pull_request_target`-equivalent risk re-implemented as a server: untrusted input processed with elevated credentials.
surviving.impact: If any analyzer Fendix shells out to (semgrep, bandit, pip dep scan) can be made to execute code or exfiltrate via a malicious repo (e.g. a poisoned setup.py / semgrep rule resolution / git submodule), the attacker reaches a context holding a token that can write check-runs, SARIF, and PR comments to every repo the App is installed in. The k8s template does drop caps + readOnlyRootFilesystem (deploy/k8s/fendix-app.yaml:62-68) which helps, but Fly.io (the documented primary deploy, deploy-app.sh/fly.toml) has no such hardening.
surviving.recommendation: Scan untrusted code in a network-isolated, unprivileged sandbox that does NOT have the installation token in its environment (clone with the token, then drop it before invoking the scanner; pass the already-cloned dir). Disable network egress for the scan subprocess. Document the trust boundary in the threat model and ensure the Fly.io deploy applies the same hardening as the k8s manifest.
surviving.verifierReasoning:
Every cited line checks out against the real code. handler.go:113-152 HandlePullRequest fires on opened/synchronize/reopened and sets cloneURL = p.PullRequest.Head.Repo.CloneURL (line 135), which for a fork PR is the attacker's fork; it falls back to Repository.CloneURL only when empty. runScan (handler.go:167-226) acquires an installation token via h.Tokens.Get (line 176) BEFORE invoking scanner.Run with that token (lines 189-193). app/manifest.yml:40-45 confirms the token scopes: security_events: write, checks: write, pull_requests: write (plus contents: read). scanner.go:100-133 injects the token into the clone URL (injectInstallationToken -> x-access-token:<token>, line 174), shallow-fetches/checks out the attacker-controlled HeadSHA, then runs `fendix scan --code <dir> --format json` over that untrusted source via exec.CommandContext (lines 125-130). There is no namespacing/seccomp/network isolation around the scan subprocess — the only bound is the 15-minute context (HandlerScanTimeout). The token lives in the clone URL, in the ScanRequest struct, and in the TokenSource cache (auth.go:226-272) for ~1h (installation tokens, IsExpired uses a 30s skew). Deploy asymmetry is real: deploy/k8s/fendix-app.yaml:62-68 drops ALL caps + readOnlyRootFilesystem + seccomp RuntimeDefault + runAsNonRoot, but fly.toml (the documented primary deploy) applies none of that container hardening. This is the pull_request_target server-equivalent: untrusted input processed in a process holding write-scoped, cross-repo credentials.

Adjustments to the finding's framing (do not refute it): (1) Webhook HMAC verification IS enforced (webhook.go:129, VerifySignature) but is irrelevant here — fork PRs from arbitrary external users produce GitHub-signed webhooks normally, so the signature gate does not stop this attack. (2) The handler/scanner do not themselves execute repo code; git fetch/checkout + fendix scan (Python AST, semgrep, dep manifest parsing) are the surface. Reaching the token requires an analyzer-level code-exec/exfil primitive (poisoned setup.py evaluation, semgrep rule resolution, git submodule hook), which is plausible for these tools but not demonstrated in this repo. (3) No code comment or threat-model documents acceptance of this untrusted-code tradeoff — the comments only cover timeouts and best-effort SARIF. Net: the architectural exposure is genuine and the medium/medium-confidence rating is appropriate — confirmed at medium. Not high because exploitation is conditional on an unproven analyzer RCE, tokens are short-lived and scoped to the App's own installations, and at least the k8s reference deploy is hardened.
surviving.falsePositiveRisk: The vulnerability is a conditional/architectural exposure, not a demonstrated RCE: it depends on one of the bundled analyzers (semgrep, bandit/Python AST, dependency manifest parser) being coercible into code execution or network exfiltration when run over an attacker-authored repo. If those analyzers are confirmed not to evaluate untrusted code (e.g. semgrep parses without executing, the Python analyzer uses ast.parse not import/exec, no submodule fetch, network egress is blocked at the platform), the practical impact collapses to DoS/resource abuse rather than token theft. Additionally, the token is per-installation and short-lived (~1h), so impact is bounded to the App's own installation set rather than all GitHub. The finding could be seen as a known design tradeoff (a code scanner inherently must read untrusted code), though no code comment documents accepting the elevated-token exposure specifically.

surviving.title: --offline / --offline-db scan flags are accepted but completely unwired (silent no-op)
surviving.description: scan registers --offline and --offline-db (main.go:397-398). Neither is read in newScanCmd's RunE, and models.ScanConfig has no Offline/OfflineDB field. The offline package only powers `fendix db update/list/verify`; per-scanner integration is deferred. So --offline does nothing and the scan still hits osv.dev/vuln.go.dev.
surviving.impact: An air-gapped operator runs `fendix scan --code . --offline --offline-db snapshot.json`, sees success, and assumes no egress — when the dep scanners actually made outbound calls (and may have silently failed/skipped, hiding CVEs). A flag promising an air-gapped guarantee but acting as a no-op manufactures false confidence in the highest-assurance deployment.
surviving.recommendation: Until per-scanner offline wiring lands, hide/remove the --offline/--offline-db scan flags (keep them on the db subcommand). If kept, fail loudly: when --offline is set, refuse any outbound request and error unless every dep scanner routes through the snapshot. Add Offline/OfflineDBPath to ScanConfig and thread them through.
surviving.verifierReasoning: Code confirms the factual core of the finding. main.go:397-398 registers flags.Bool("offline",...) and flags.String("offline-db",...). newScanCmd's RunE (main.go:204-302) reads ~30 flags into models.ScanConfig but never calls flags.GetBool("offline") or flags.GetString("offline-db") — the two flags are never consulted. internal/models/config.go ScanConfig (lines 1-97) has no Offline/OfflineDB field; grep for "Offline" across the entire internal/ tree returns zero hits. The offline package is imported only by cmd/fendix/db.go (db update/list/verify), and db.go:23 explicitly documents the scan-time --offline integration as pending. The dep scanners that execute during a --code scan make real egress with no offline gate: internal/scanner/deps/npm/scanner.go:67 and pip/scanner.go:81 set osvAPIBase="https://api.osv.dev" and POST to /v1/query[batch] (npm:305/505, pip:439/749); govulncheck/scanner.go:46 defaults to https://vuln.go.dev. No FENDIX_OFFLINE env var or proxy gate exists. These scanners are registered in internal/engine/orchestrator.go, which newScanCmd invokes via engine.NewOrchestrator(cfg).Run(ctx). So `fendix scan --code . --offline --offline-db snap.json` does make outbound calls and the flag is a true no-op. The factual claim is fully supported. I downgrade severity from high to medium for impact calibration, not because the bug is absent: the flag's help text is unusually candid — it literally states "Today this is a no-op honest stub ... per-scanner integration is wired sprint-by-sprint" and --offline-db says "Only effective with --offline." This is a documented, in-progress Sprint-09 feature with truthful self-disclosure, not a covert/hidden security control that falsely claims enforcement. An operator who reads --help is told it does nothing. The residual risk (a busy air-gapped operator infers air-gapped behavior from the flag name without reading the long help string, then sees dep checks silently fail/skip and assumes no CVEs) is genuine and operationally meaningful, which keeps it above low/info, but the explicit no-op documentation rules out the "manufactures false confidence in a high-assurance control" framing that would justify high.
surviving.falsePositiveRisk: The flag is not silently broken — its help text openly states it is a "no-op honest stub" and that integration is pending, so a strict reading is that this is a documented unimplemented feature rather than a security defect, which could make the high-severity "false air-gap guarantee" framing a false positive. Additionally, an air-gapped runner with no network route would have the dep scanners' HTTP POSTs simply fail/time out (egress blocked at the perimeter), so the worst-case data-exfil concern is largely theoretical in a true air gap; the practical harm reduces to confusing failure modes and possibly missed/incomplete CVE results rather than guaranteed silent egress.

surviving.title: check_run rerequested path reuses the same unvalidated HeadSHA + repo clone_url into git
surviving.description: HandleCheckRun (action=rerequested) extracts `p.CheckRun.HeadSHA` and `p.Repository.CloneURL` from the webhook and passes them to the shared runScan → FendixScanner.Run path with no validation, identical to the pull_request path. This is the same git-fetch argument-injection sink as finding ghapp-headsha-git-arg-injection but reachable through a second event type (the GitHub UI 'Re-run check' button, whose payload an attacker can influence for a check on their fork's commit). Listed separately because it is a distinct, independently-reachable entry point that a fix on only the pull_request handler would miss.
surviving.impact: Second code path to the same RCE-on-host sink; ensures the vulnerability is not closed by patching only HandlePullRequest.
surviving.recommendation: Centralise HeadSHA hex-validation (and clone-URL host pinning) inside runScan / FendixScanner.Run so every event entry point (pull_request, check_run, and any future one) is covered by a single fail-closed check.
surviving.verifierReasoning:
The cited code exists exactly as quoted: HandleCheckRun (handler.go:298-306) passes p.CheckRun.HeadSHA and p.Repository.CloneURL into the shared runScan -> Scanner.Run path with no SHA-format validation, mirroring HandlePullRequest. That much is accurate. But the finding's security characterization is overstated and, more importantly, it is the same sink reached via a second router case, not a new vulnerability.

Sink analysis (scanner.go:105-160, 178-186): the git steps are executed via exec.CommandContext(ctx, name, args...) — Go os/exec with an argv slice and NO shell. Classic command injection (;, |, $(), backticks) is categorically impossible, so the claimed category=command-injection and impact "RCE on host" are not supported. CloneURL is validated by injectInstallationToken -> url.Parse with a mandatory u.Scheme=="https" check (scanner.go:166-176); non-URL/non-https values are rejected before any git invocation. HeadSHA is passed as the final positional argument after "origin" in `git fetch --quiet --depth=1 origin <HeadSHA>`, i.e. in refspec position where git treats it as a refspec, not as a global option — the realistic worst case is git rejecting a malformed refspec, not arbitrary option/RCE.

Controllability: ServeHTTP enforces VerifySignature (HMAC-SHA256 over the body with the App secret) before dispatch (webhook.go:129-138), and the only caller wiring is cmd/fendix-app/main.go via NewServer/NewHandler — there is no API or other path feeding arbitrary head_sha. So the payload values come from GitHub, not directly from the attacker. check_run.head_sha is a commit SHA that GitHub computes as a cryptographic hash; an attacker controls commit content on their fork but cannot make GitHub emit a head_sha string like "--upload-pack=...". The finding's premise that "an attacker can influence the payload" to inject a crafted SHA string is therefore materially weaker than stated.

Duplicate framing: the finding explicitly cross-references ghapp-headsha-git-arg-injection and admits "this is the same git-fetch argument-injection sink ... reachable through a second event type." The validation gap and the git sink are identical and both live in the shared Scanner.Run, not in HandlePullRequest. The finding's stated justification — "a fix on only the pull_request handler would miss it" — is wrong: the fix point is Scanner.Run (e.g. enforce ^[0-9a-f]{40,64}$ on HeadSHA, or add a `--` end-of-options separator), and any such fix closes both event paths at once. So this is a duplicate of the parent sink reached via a different webhook event, with no independent sink or independent validation gap.

The threat-model.md covers only the active scanner; it does not address this webhook git path, so it is neither documented nor an accepted tradeoff. On its own merits the residual issue is at most a low-severity defense-in-depth gap (no strict hex-SHA validation before git fetch), not a high-severity, independently-reachable RCE.
surviving.falsePositiveRisk: If a future code path ever feeds head_sha/clone_url from a non-GitHub, attacker-controlled source (e.g. a manual re-scan API), or if the parent finding is treated as not-yet-tracked, then this entry point's lack of SHA validation would be a genuine (though still non-shell, argument-injection-at-most) issue worth hardening. Also, GitHub's exact guarantees on head_sha character set are an external assumption; if GitHub ever delivered a non-hex head_sha it would reach git unvalidated. surviving.title: Unicode bidi/RTL control characters in finding fields are not stripped, enabling report-content spoofing in HTML and PDF reports
surviving.description: Finding fields (Title, Evidence, Fix, Endpoint, Category, AffectedEndpoints, TaintChain.Expr) come from scanning untrusted targets and are rendered verbatim into the HTML report via html/template. html/template HTML-escapes <, >, &, quotes but does NOT strip Unicode bidirectional control characters (U+202A..U+202E LRE/RLE/PDF/LRO/RLO, U+2066..U+2069 LRI/RLI/FSI/PDI). An attacker controlling a scanned response (a reflected value, a server header, an error page string, a JS source snippet) can embed RLO/LRO overrides so the rendered finding title/evidence reads differently from its logical bytes. The RTL CSS branch (lines 22-27) and the Arabic locale make bidi rendering the norm for ar reports, but the spoofing payload lives in the per-finding data itself, so it affects English (LTR) reports too via explicit override codepoints, independent of the operator-controlled .Lang/.RTL switch.
surviving.impact: An operator reviewing an HTML or PDF report can be deceived about which endpoint a finding affects, what the evidence says, or the severity context (a real critical issue disguised as informational, or a malicious URL/endpoint visually masked). In an enterprise triage workflow where reports drive remediation prioritisation and are forwarded to auditors, this lets a compromised or adversarial scan target manipulate the human decision. SARIF Message/Name and PDF cells carry the same un-sanitised text.
surviving.recommendation: Before rendering, sanitise finding text fields by stripping or visibly escaping Unicode bidi control characters (U+202A-U+202E and U+2066-U+2069, plus U+200E/U+200F if unneeded). Do this in a shared normalisation step (extend SanitizeFindings or add a NeutralizeBidi helper) applied to Title, Evidence, Fix, Endpoint, AffectedEndpoints, Category, and TaintChain.Expr for ALL report formats. Replacing bidi controls with visible \uXXXX escapes (or U+FFFD) preserves the literal content while preventing visual reordering.

The core mechanism is real and the cited lines exist. I verified empirically that U+202A/U+202E/U+2066/U+2069 are all >= 0x2000, i.e. NOT < 32. I traced the only sanitization in the pipeline: reporters.SanitizeFindings (sanitize.go, called at orchestrator.go:456) only string-replaces auth credential values with [REDACTED] on Evidence/Fix/Title; it does no bidi/control stripping. The single place control chars are removed is sanitizeConfigLeakEvidence (configleak.go:228-236), which (a) is scoped to the config-leak scanner's evidence only and (b) only drops runes with r < 32 — bidi overrides survive it. So no guard handles this case. Attacker-controlled, untrusted scan-target content reaches the raw fields: headers.go:126 Evidence "Server: %s" and headers.go:147 "X-Powered-By: %s" embed the verbatim response-header value with %s (no escaping); cors.go:97 reflects an attacker origin; Endpoint/Title fields (e.g. semgrep/textscan/configleak titles, endpoint.FullURL) are raw. A malicious target returning a Server header containing U+202E will land that codepoint unmodified in
{{.Evidence}}

surviving.title: C0/C1 and zero-width control characters in finding fields pass through html/template unescaped, allowing content hiding/obfuscation in reports
surviving.description: Beyond bidi overrides, html/template does not remove zero-width (U+200B ZWSP, U+FEFF BOM, U+200C/U+200D ZWJ/ZWNJ) or other non-printing control characters embedded in attacker-controlled finding fields. These render verbatim into Title/Evidence/Endpoint and the data-endpoint/data-source attributes (line 114) used by the client-side sort JS. An attacker-controlled scan target can pad strings with zero-width characters so two byte-distinct findings collapse visually, or so an operator's in-report Ctrl-F search fails to match a malicious endpoint. The slug() function in sarif.go drops these for rule IDs, but the SARIF Name/Message text fields (sarif.go lines 223,244) do not.
surviving.impact: Lower-severity obfuscation / anti-triage: an operator may miss or misread a finding because zero-width characters defeat in-report search and visual de-duplication. Combined with bidi spoofing this strengthens the report-manipulation vector. Not code execution.
surviving.recommendation: In the same normalisation pass recommended for bidi controls, also strip C0/C1 control characters (except intended \t/\n) and zero-width formatting characters from human-facing finding fields before rendering. Apply uniformly across HTML, PDF, and SARIF text fields.

surviving.title: Attacker-controlled scan data is written into SARIF artifactLocation.uri, logicalLocation.name, message/help text, and tags without validation, exposing downstream SARIF consumers
surviving.description: RenderSARIF copies untrusted finding data verbatim into the SARIF document: rule Name/ShortDescription/Help from f.Title and f.Fix (lines 222-224), Properties.Tags directly from f.References (line 229), result Message from f.Evidence (line 244), physicalLocation artifactLocation.uri from parseLine(f.Line) (line 255), and logicalLocation.name from f.Endpoint / f.AffectedEndpoints (line 275). encoding/json correctly escapes these so the SARIF stays structurally valid, but the VALUES are unconstrained attacker-influenced strings. SARIF is consumed by privileged UIs: GitHub Code Scanning renders message text and turns location URIs into clickable links / file annotations, and IDE SARIF viewers resolve artifactLocation.uri against the workspace. helpUri is filtered to http/https only (lines 169-182, a good control), but artifactLocation.uri and the location/name fields have no such filter, so a malicious target can inject crafted file-path URIs (../, absolute paths) a viewer resolves, place arbitrary trusted-looking message text, or feed References into Tags/helpUri.
surviving.impact: When the SARIF is uploaded to GitHub Code Scanning or opened in an enterprise SARIF viewer, attacker-controlled scan data drives clickable links, file annotations, and trusted message text in the security dashboard, enabling phishing-style links, misleading annotations on arbitrary file paths, or path-traversal-style URIs the viewer resolves. Because CI/operators trust Fendix output, this is a confused-deputy injection into downstream security tooling.
surviving.recommendation: Validate/normalise location URIs before emitting: ensure artifactLocation.uri is a relative path with no scheme and no traversal (reject or escape absolute paths, ../ and URL schemes), or emit it as uriBaseId-relative. Apply the same http/https allowlist used for helpUri to any reference surfaced as a link. Strip control/bidi characters from Message/Name/Help text. Document that downstream consumers must treat these fields as untrusted.
surviving.verifierReasoning:
The cited code exists exactly as described in go/internal/reporters/sarif.go. Verbatim copies confirmed: Name/ShortDescription = f.Title and Help = f.Fix (lines 222-224); Tags = f.References (line 229); result Message = f.Evidence (line 244); artifactLocation.uri = filePath from parseLine(f.Line) (line 255); logicalLocation.name = ep (lines 275-276). The only URI/scheme control is sarifHelpURI (lines 169-182, http/https/CWE-only) and it applies ONLY to helpUri, so the asymmetry the finding claims is real. The single pre-render guard, reporters.SanitizeFindings (sanitize.go), only string-replaces known auth credential values (auth.Value / Bearer / Basic tokens) in Evidence/Fix/Title; it does no URI, path, scheme, or length validation and does not touch References or endpoints, so no existing guard handles these vectors. Both render paths (orchestrator.go:533 after SanitizeFindings, and cmd/fendix/main.go:458 re-rendering a saved JSON report) feed values through unchanged.

The premise that values are attacker-influenced is partially supported. Evidence genuinely embeds target-controlled response data (configleak.go:147 body sample, headers.go:126 Server header, cors.go:97 reflected attacker origin, injection.go response/error signatures). Endpoint/logicalLocation.name can come from crawler-discovered paths (crawler.go HTML-link/robots/sitemap/JS discovery, lines 466-579), which the target server influences. So injecting misleading text and odd location LABELS into a SARIF consumer is realistic.

However the writeup's two highest-impact claims are weak. (1) artifactLocation.uri is fed only from f.Line, which is set exclusively by whitebox/SAST scanners (semgrep, secrets, deps, textscan, configleak) over the operator's own local code or dependency metadata — not from remote crawl data — so the "../ / absolute-path URI a viewer resolves" path-traversal vector requires the target to control a local code file path, which does not occur in normal blackbox scanning; the strongest realistic input is malicious third-party dependency metadata. (2) References->Tags/helpUri is largely refuted: first-party scanners hardcode References as CWE/OWASP constants (e.g. cors.go:75 []string{"CWE-942"}), and dependency scanners populate them from trusted OSV IDs (v.ID / v.Aliases[0], e.g. GHSA-/CVE- ids in npm/scanner.go:548) — none are URLs, so they never pass the http/https prefix check in sarifHelpURI and cannot become a clickable phishing helpUri; they only become plain tag strings. Also, GitHub Code Scanning renders message.text as plain text (not active HTML/links) and logicalLocation.name is a non-resolvable label, so the "clickable phishing links / file annotations on arbitrary paths" impact is overstated.

Net: the structural defect (untrusted-influenced text/label values copied verbatim with no validation, asymmetric to the filtered helpUri) is genuinely present and unguarded, so the finding is confirmed rather than refuted. But real exploitability is a report-hygiene / defense-in-depth nuisance (misleading text and location labels in a dashboard), not a confused-deputy URI-injection: the one unfiltered field that is remote-influenced is a label/text, and the only freely-resolvable URI field is sourced from local code. Adjusting medium -> low.
surviving.falsePositiveRisk: The verbatim copying and missing validation are objectively real, but the "downstream privileged tooling" impact is largely theoretical: GitHub Code Scanning treats message.text as inert plain text, logicalLocation.name is a non-resolvable label, References are hardcoded constants or trusted OSV IDs that cannot reach the filtered helpUri, and the only freely-resolvable URI field (artifactLocation.uri) is sourced from operator-local code paths, not remote attacker input. A reasonable maintainer could classify this as accepted output-rendering behavior (SARIF is trusted scanner output by design), making the security-relevance borderline.

surviving.title: PDF reporter uses fpdf built-in Latin-1 fonts with no bidi handling; non-Latin/RTL finding text is silently mangled and bidi controls are not neutralised
surviving.description: RenderPDF feeds untrusted finding fields (f.Title, f.Fix, f.Endpoint, f.Severity, f.Confidence) directly into fpdf CellFormat/MultiCell using built-in Helvetica (lines 153, 195-200, 228-235). fpdf standard fonts are Latin-1 only; the code's own comment (lines 308-322) acknowledges glyph substitution for non-Latin-1 input and defers a Unicode font to a later sprint. truncatePDFLine is rune-aware (no mid-byte split), but there is no neutralisation of bidi/zero-width control characters and no transliteration, so attacker-supplied RTL/control-laden text in a title/fix is rendered as substituted/garbage glyphs or with undefined ordering. fpdf does not execute embedded content (no PDF-JS / launch-action sink here, so this is not active PDF content injection), but the executive PDF is the artifact most likely forwarded to non-technical stakeholders, so silent corruption/spoofing of finding text undermines its trustworthiness.
surviving.impact: Finding titles/fixes containing non-Latin or control characters (legitimately from Arabic targets, or maliciously from a crafted target) render incorrectly or unreadably in the executive PDF, and bidi overrides can visually reorder Latin text, letting an attacker degrade or spoof the human-facing executive report. No code execution.
surviving.recommendation: Apply the shared bidi/control-character neutralisation to all strings passed to fpdf, and either register a Unicode (Noto) font with proper shaping/bidi before shipping Arabic/RTL PDF support, or explicitly transliterate/replace un-renderable runes with a visible placeholder rather than relying on fpdf silent substitution. Until then, document that PDF output is English/Latin-only.

(3) truncatePDFLine (313-322) is rune-aware (utf8.RuneCountInString, []rune slice) so no mid-byte split, but it performs NO stripping of bidi overrides (U+202A-202E, U+2066-2069), zero-width chars, or other control characters, and no transliteration. surviving.title: CheckInjection ignores ctx cancellation between probes — probes keep firing after budget/duration soft-stop
surviving.description: The worker pool only checks ctx.Done() between jobs (workerpool.go:67-71) and before sending results (75-79). Once a CheckInjection job starts, CheckInjectionWithAudit loops over every (param, location) target and unconditionally calls probeSQLi/probeSQLiErrorBased/probeSQLiBoolean/probeCMDi/probeCRLF (injection.go:366-383). None of those, nor the per-payload loop in probeSQLi (401), nor measureBaseline's 3-request loop (141), select on ctx.Done() between requests. Contrast ratelimit.go:69-72 which correctly checks `case <-ctx.Done()` inside its burst loop. So after MaxDuration deadline fires or MaxRequests cap trips cancelBudget, an in-progress endpoint with up to MaxProbesPerEndpoint (default 20) targets keeps iterating. The soft-stop is partially saved by two side effects — budget.Transport rejects over-cap requests instantly with ErrBudgetExceeded, and a deadline-cancelled ctx makes client.Do return immediately — but the loop still walks every remaining probe doing per-iteration work (building requests, measureBaseline failing 3x, Record() writes, logagg.Warn spam) instead of returning promptly.
surviving.impact: Defeats the 'in-flight requests finish, no new ones start' soft-stop promise (orchestrator.go:115-122) at the per-endpoint granularity: with active probing enabled, a scan can keep doing work and emitting [PROBE]/WARN lines well past --max-duration, and a single slow endpoint extends the scan past its deadline. Also produces misleading audit records (status=0 'request failed') for the post-cancellation probes.
surviving.recommendation: Add `select { case <-ctx.Done(): return findings; default: }` at the top of the target loop in CheckInjectionWithAudit and inside the payload loop in probeSQLi/measureBaseline, mirroring ratelimit.go. Bail the whole check as soon as ctx.Err() != nil.

(2) The worker pool only checks ctx between jobs (workerpool.go:67-71) and before sending results (75-79); once job.check(ctx,...) is called at line 73, CheckInjectionWithAudit runs to completion. (3) CheckInjectionWithAudit (injection.go:366-383) loops every (param,location) target and unconditionally calls probeSQLi/probeSQLiErrorBased/probeSQLiBoolean/probeCMDi/probeCRLF; the only loop guard is the audit-count vs maxProbes budget (367, 402-404, 508, 583, 663, 734), never ctx. (4) measureBaseline (138-157) does 3 sequential client.Do calls with no ctx check between them. All true.

However the finding itself correctly credits the two guards that contain the blast radius, and re-reading the budget package confirms them as decisive: budgetTransport.RoundTrip (budget.go:101-114) does sent.Add(1) then, if over cap, returns ErrBudgetExceeded WITHOUT any network I/O — so post-cap probes never hit the wire. And every probe builds its request with NewRequestWithContext(ctx,...) (buildProbeRequest 286-316, probeCRLF 746, measureBaseline 142), so once --max-duration cancels ctx, client.Do returns immediately with a context error. What leaks past cancellation is only wasted local work: the loop walks remaining targets of the one in-progress endpoint per worker (bounded by MaxProbesPerEndpoint, default 20 — injection.go:27), each doing fast-failing client.Do calls, writing status=0 ProbeRecords, and emitting logagg.Warn (which is volume-capped/aggregated — orchestrator.go:78-82, logagg.Summary). No attacker input drives this; it is a self-imposed scan-control feature, not a vulnerability boundary. The documented contract (CHANGELOG:1925, orchestrator.go:121-122, TASK-095 note) is explicitly job-scheduling-granular — 'stops scheduling new jobs' / 'in-flight requests finish' — which the implementation actually honors; the finding judges the promise at a finer per-probe granularity than the code ever claimed. surviving.title: Deduplicate keeps the first-seen finding as primary, and first-seen order is the nondeterministic worker-completion order
surviving.description: Deduplicate groups by dedupKey (severity|category|title) and keeps `primary = first-seen finding`, preserving that finding's Evidence, Fix, Line, TaintChain, etc (54-63). AffectedEndpoints is sorted (90) so that field is stable, but the primary's narrative fields are not. The later sort.Slice (382) is also non-stable (sort.Slice, not SliceStable), so even findings sharing the full (endpoint,category,title) key can reorder, though that only matters for ID assignment ties.
