surviving.title: Native dep/secrets/semgrep/textscan failures are logged at WARN and swallowed — silent coverage loss with exit 0
surviving.description: Every native scanner's non-sentinel error path is `default: slog.Warn(...); continue` — govulncheck (215), pip (244), npm (271), secrets (289), semgrep (310), textscan (320). A genuine failure (e.g. govulncheck couldn't build the module, OSV.dev returned 5xx, semgrep crashed mid-run) produces zero findings from that scanner, a single WARN line, and the scan proceeds to exit 0 / exit-by-fail-on as if that surface were clean. There is no signal in the report JSON/SARIF that a scanner was attempted-and-failed vs. attempted-and-found-nothing. The Python whitebox path is slightly better (it returns partial findings on error, spawner.go:138-144 / orchestrator.go:686-690) but still only Error-logs.
surviving.impact: In CI, a transient network or tooling failure silently degrades a security scan to a clean-looking pass — the worst failure mode for a gate that teams trust to block vulnerable deps/secrets. An attacker or a flaky environment can hide CVEs/secrets behind a WARN that nobody reads.
surviving.recommendation: Track per-scanner status in ScanMetadata (e.g. scanner_errors []{name, error}) and surface it in the report and the 'scan complete' summary. Consider an opt-in --fail-on-scanner-error (or making it the default in CI mode) so a scanner that errored out fails the build instead of passing silently. At minimum emit the failures into the report metadata so SARIF/JSON consumers can detect incomplete coverage.
surviving.verifierReasoning:
Re-read go/internal/engine/orchestrator.go. Every load-bearing claim holds:

1. Native scanner non-sentinel error paths are plain `slog.Warn(...)` followed by fall-through, with no findings appended and no error propagation:

   - pip: line 243-244 `default: slog.Warn("native pypi deps scan failed", "error", err)`
   - npm: line 270-271 `default: slog.Warn("native npm deps scan failed", "error", err)`
   - secrets: line 288-289 `default: slog.Warn("native secrets scan failed", "error", err)`
   - semgrep: line 309-310 `default: slog.Warn("native semgrep scan failed", "error", err)`
   - textscan: line 320-321 `if err != nil { slog.Warn("native textscan failed", "error", err) }`
   All exactly as cited.

2. Fail-open at exit: checkFailOn (lines 544-561) iterates only over findings and returns 1 only if a finding meets/exceeds the threshold. A scanner that errors contributes zero findings, so it cannot raise the exit code. Scan() returns checkFailOn(findings) (line 514). Confirmed: a govulncheck build failure / OSV 5xx / semgrep crash leaves exit 0 (or exit-by-fail-on driven purely by the other surfaces) — the gate looks clean.

3. No report signal for attempted-and-failed vs attempted-and-clean. ScanMetadata (lines 437-446) carries ChecksRun (lines 423-435), which is populated unconditionally based on config flags (`if o.cfg.CodePath != "" { checksRun = append(... "secrets","semgrep","deps") }`) — it records intent, not outcome. There is no per-scanner status/error field, so a failed scanner is indistinguishable from a clean one in the JSON/SARIF output. Severity assessment: this is a genuine fail-open weakness in a security gate, and the impact narrative (transient infra/tooling failure silently degrading a trusted CI gate to a clean pass) is real and correctly framed. The category label "report-injection" is a poor fit (this is really fail-open / silent-degradation / missing-error-propagation, not injection), but that is a taxonomy quibble, not a correctness issue. Exploitability is limited: the failure trigger (transient network/tooling error) is generally not attacker-controlled, and the failure is visible to anyone watching WARN-level logs, so a diligent CI setup that fails on WARN or scrapes logs would catch it. surviving.title: Deduplicate.mergeSource comment claims black+white groups 'were already merged by Correlate' — not guaranteed; attribution can be wrong
surviving.description: mergeSource's contract comment (lines 26-30 and 122-125) asserts that a mix of blackbox + whitebox in a dedup group without an existing correlated entry 'would have been merged by Correlate already, so this fallback only matters for same-source groups.' Two findings that share a dedup key but live on different endpoints will NOT be correlated, so a blackbox and a whitebox finding with identical (severity,category,title) on different endpoints reach Deduplicate uncorrelated and DO hit the cross-source mergeSource branch (returns SourceBlackbox). The chosen behavior (blackbox wins) is defensible, but the justifying comment is wrong and could mislead a future maintainer into removing the branch.
surviving.impact: Low direct impact — output is reasonable — but the incorrect invariant in the comment is a latent correctness trap; someone trusting it might simplify mergeSource and mis-attribute a merged finding's Source (which feeds report grouping and the correlated/blackbox/whitebox UX).
surviving.recommendation: Fix the comment to state the real invariant: cross-source groups CAN occur here (same title/severity/category on different endpoints that Correlate never paired), and mergeSource deliberately picks the most-trusted source. Keep the branch.

surviving.title: Deeply-nested YAML/JSON spec throws RecursionError that bypasses check_auth's error handling
surviving.description: check_auth() wraps self.load() in `except (OSError, yaml.YAMLError, json.JSONDecodeError, ValueError)`. A spec with deeply-nested flow collections (e.g. `[[[[...]]]]` thousands deep) makes yaml.safe_load / json.loads raise RecursionError, which is a RuntimeError subclass and is NOT in that tuple. Reproduced end-to-end: feeding such a spec yields stderr `check 'auth (spec)' failed: maximum recursion depth exceeded` and the engine emits zero auth findings instead of the intended SEC-SPEC-PARSE 'spec could not be parsed' finding. The engine survives (engine._run_check catches Exception) but the diagnostic finding the parser is designed to emit for a bad spec is lost.
surviving.impact: A malformed/malicious spec silently produces no auth analysis and no parse-error finding — the operator cannot tell whether the API was analyzed-and-clean or never-parsed. Combined with the missing size cap (see spec-no-size-cap) this is the spec-side analogue of the AST suppression issue.
surviving.recommendation: Broaden the except in check_auth to also catch RecursionError (or use `except Exception`) and emit SEC-SPEC-PARSE. Consider bumping sys.setrecursionlimit guard or pre-validating nesting depth before parse.
surviving.verifierReasoning: The cited code is accurate. spec_parser.py:67-69 wraps self.load() in `except (OSError, yaml.YAMLError, json.JSONDecodeError, ValueError)`. I verified programmatically that RecursionError is a RuntimeError subclass and is NOT a subclass of OSError/ValueError, so it is not caught by that tuple. yaml.safe_load on a deeply-nested flow collection ('['*60000 + ']'*60000) raises RecursionError — reproduced end-to-end through SpecParser.check_auth: it raised RecursionError and emitted 0 findings, never reaching the SEC-SPEC-PARSE emit_fn. The default recursion limit is 1000 and the existing fuzz test (test_fuzz.py:111 test_deeply_nested_yaml) only goes 50 levels deep, so this depth is genuinely unguarded. The engine survives because engine.py:34 _run_check catches `except Exception` and logs to stderr, but the operator-facing parse-error diagnostic finding is silently dropped — exactly the claimed behavior. CORRECTION to the finding: the JSON-path claim is false. Python's json.loads uses an iterative C scanner; I parsed 50000-deep nested arrays with no RecursionError. Only the YAML path is affected. I downgrade severity from medium to low: this is a missing-diagnostic / observability bug, not a security bypass or DoS. The engine does not crash, the scan completes, and a stderr log line ("check 'auth (spec)' failed: maximum recursion depth exceeded") is produced — so the operator is not entirely blind, though the structured SEC-SPEC-PARSE finding is missing. Real exploitability is low: it only fires on a hand-crafted malicious/malformed spec the operator themselves supplied as a scan target, there is no untrusted-input amplification, and worst case is a lost diagnostic finding plus a stderr message. Genuine but minor robustness/consistency gap relative to the parser's stated 'always emit a parse-error finding' contract.
surviving.falsePositiveRisk: The impact is partially mitigated by the stderr log line from _run_check, so an attentive operator monitoring stderr would see the failure — the claim of being fully 'unable to tell' overstates the blindness. Also the finding's JSON claim is incorrect (json.loads does not recurse), so one of the two cited triggers does not exist. The remaining YAML trigger requires the operator to point the scanner at an adversarial spec they control, with no privilege escalation or service impact, which is closer to a hardening/robustness gap than a security finding.

surviving.title: SpecParser fetches arbitrary URLs (SSRF) with redirect-following and no response size cap
surviving.description: _parse_file() treats any spec_path beginning with http:// or https:// as a remote URL and calls urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=30) (the `# noqa: S310` shows the bandit SSRF warning was knowingly suppressed). There is no allow-list of hosts/schemes beyond the http(s) prefix check, redirects are followed by default (urllib's default opener), and resp.read() is unbounded — the entire body is decoded into memory. Although the spec path is operator-supplied via --spec (not attacker-derived in the ghapp flow), the fetch runs inside the engine subprocess with the engine's network identity.
surviving.impact: If a fendix invocation ever lets a less-trusted caller influence --spec (CI matrix, server mode, future automation), this becomes a server-side request forgery primitive that can reach cloud metadata (169.254.169.254), internal RFC1918 services, or file://-redirect targets, and a hostile/large endpoint can OOM the engine via an unbounded response body. Defense-in-depth gap even with an operator-controlled URL.
surviving.recommendation: Restrict to https only (or an explicit allow-list), disable automatic redirects or re-validate each redirect target against the allow-list, block link-local/loopback/RFC1918 destinations, and cap resp.read() to a maximum byte count (e.g. read(MAX+1) and reject if exceeded).
surviving.verifierReasoning:
The cited code is real and reachable. python/analyzers/spec_parser.py:270-279 does exactly what is claimed: if spec_path starts with http://|https:// it builds a urllib.request.Request and calls urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=30)  # noqa: S310, follows redirects via the default opener, and does an unbounded resp.read().decode("utf-8") with no size cap or host/scheme allowlist beyond the prefix check. It is live code, not dead: go/internal/engine/orchestrator.go:679 sets Spec via absPathOrEmpty(), which (lines 640-655) DELIBERATELY preserves http(s):// URLs unchanged ("URLs must not be passed through filepath.Abs"), and python/engine.py:50 reads request["spec"] into spec_path then constructs SpecParser(spec_path).check_auth(...) when "auth" in checks. So an operator-supplied --spec URL does reach urlopen.

However, the SSRF severity (medium, "reach 169.254.169.254 / RFC1918 / file:// redirects") is overstated and effectively refuted on exploitability grounds:

1. Threat model: the ONLY untrusted-input flow is the GitHub App webhook path (go/internal/ghapp/scanner.go:124-129), which invokes fendixBin with "scan","--code",dir,"--format","json","--output",findingsPath — it NEVER passes --spec and never derives a spec path from PR/webhook content. The spec path is purely operator/CLI-supplied (main.go:207/276/365). The finding itself concedes this. So SSRF is not reachable from attacker-controlled input in any shipped flow; the impact is entirely conditional on a hypothetical future caller ("if fendix ever lets a less-trusted caller influence --spec").

2. "No allowlist" is the accepted design, not a Python-specific bug: the Go sibling loadSpec/fetchSpec (crawler.go:331-392) likewise has NO host allowlist and no RFC1918/metadata-IP blocking. Both paths trust the operator-supplied --spec by design. file:// is NOT reachable — the prefix gate only enters urlopen for http(s), and a 3xx redirect to file:// is not followed to the local filesystem by urllib's HTTP redirect handler (it stays within HTTP redirect handling).

The one genuinely valid, concrete, asymmetric gap is the missing response-size cap: the Go fetchSpec hardens the identical fetch with const maxSpecBytes = 50<<20 using io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(resp.Body, maxSpecBytes+1)) plus an explicit length check (crawler.go:363-370), while the Python twin does an unbounded resp.read(). An operator pointing --spec at a hostile/huge endpoint could OOM the engine subprocess. That is a real defense-in-depth / cross-implementation-consistency gap worth fixing (add a LimitReader-equivalent cap and decode the bounded bytes), but it is operator-triggered, self-inflicted, and bounded to a subprocess — hence low, not medium.
surviving.falsePositiveRisk: The SSRF/metadata framing is essentially a false positive for the shipped product: --spec is never attacker-influenced (ghapp passes only --code), and the "no allowlist" property is shared with and accepted in the Go implementation, indicating an intentional operator-trust model rather than an oversight. The only defensible residual issue is the unbounded resp.read() (no size cap), which the Go path explicitly caps at 50MB; even that requires an operator to point --spec at a hostile endpoint, so real-world impact is minor. If the reviewer's environment never exposes --spec to less-trusted callers, the residual risk is near zero.

surviving.title: Manifest and local-spec reads have no size cap (memory exhaustion)
surviving.description: DepsAnalyzer reads requirements.txt and package.json with Path.read_text(encoding='utf-8') and no size guard, then _parse_package_json runs json.loads over the whole string. spec_parser._parse_file similarly does path.read_text() with no cap (line 282). This is inconsistent with ast_analyzer.py which enforces _MAX_FILE_BYTES = 1MB (lines 105, 124) before reading. A multi-hundred-MB requirements.txt / package.json / spec in a scanned repo is loaded fully into the engine's memory.
surviving.impact: A hostile repo can commit a huge manifest or spec to balloon the engine's RSS and cause an OOM kill; the Go side interprets the killed/exited subprocess as a scan failure (spawner.go waitErr path). Lower severity because it requires an oversized file in the scanned tree and only degrades availability of the deps/spec pass.
surviving.recommendation: Apply the same _MAX_FILE_BYTES stat-check guard used in ast_analyzer to deps.py manifest reads and to spec_parser local-file reads before read_text(); skip + log files over the cap.
surviving.verifierReasoning: All cited code verified as described. deps.py:275 reads requirements.txt via `text = req_file.read_text(encoding="utf-8")` then `_parse_requirements(text)` with no size guard. deps.py:429 reads package.json via `text = pkg_file.read_text(encoding="utf-8")` then `_parse_package_json(text)`, and `_parse_package_json` (lines 208-219) calls `json.loads(text)` on the entire string. spec_parser.py:282 reads local specs via `text = path.read_text(encoding="utf-8")` then `json.loads`/`yaml.safe_load` with no cap. No upstream guard exists: engine.py (lines 49-92) passes code_path/spec straight through, and grep found no setrlimit/RLIMIT/cgroup/ulimit anywhere in python/ or the Go spawner. The impact path is also accurate: spawner.go:118 `waitErr := cmd.Wait()` and lines 138-143 convert a non-zero/SIGKILL exit (what an OOM kill produces) into `SpawnResult{Err: ...}`, i.e. a scan failure. These factors keep it at low severity; some deployments with adequate container limits or pre-scan size gating may consider it effectively non-exploitable.

surviving.title: Symlinked source files are read and a matched line can surface in findings (arbitrary file read)
surviving.description: os.walk does not recurse into symlinked directories (default followlinks=False), but a symlinked *file* inside the scanned tree with a .py/.js/.ts/.jsx/.tsx suffix is still enumerated and read via read_text. The Python path puts the matched source line (_line_text -> evidence) into the finding; the JS path puts line.strip()[:200] into evidence. Reproduced: a `.py` symlink to /etc/hosts is enumerated by os.walk. Content only leaks into a finding when a line happens to match a dangerous-call pattern, so the leak is constrained, but the engine will read any symlink-reachable file regardless of whether it lives outside the intended scan root.
surviving.impact: A crafted repo (e.g. attacker PR) can plant symlinks pointing outside the checkout; if any reachable line matches a sink pattern, up to 200 chars of an out-of-tree file appears verbatim in the report's `evidence`/`taint_chain` fields. Bounded data exposure rather than full file read.
surviving.recommendation: Skip symlinked entries (fpath.is_symlink()) during the walk, or resolve each file with Path.resolve() and confirm it is still under the scan root before reading — mirror the path-traversal guidance the analyzer itself emits in its CWE-22 fix text.
surviving.verifierReasoning:
The cited code exists verbatim and the mechanism reproduces end-to-end. In python/analyzers/ast_analyzer.py:85 `for dirpath, dirnames, filenames in os.walk(root):` uses os.walk with the default followlinks=False, and dirnames is pruned (line 86) only for _SKIP_DIRS — there is no symlink check on files. A symlinked file is still enumerated (line 88), its suffix is matched (lines 91-94), and the content is read via filepath.read_text (line 107 Python / line 126 JS). I empirically confirmed: an `os.walk` over a dir containing `leak.py -> /etc/hosts` enumerates the symlink (is_symlink=True) and read_text returns /etc/hosts content. I then ran the real ASTAnalyzer against a repo whose only .py file was a symlink to an out-of-tree file `/tmp/symtest2/outside_secret.py`; the finding emitted with endpoint `innocuous.py:2` and evidence exactly `result = eval(API_TOKEN)` — i.e. a line from a file outside the scan root surfaced verbatim in the report. The Python path puts the matched line into `evidence` via _line_text (lines 200-204, 225); the JS path via line.strip()[:200] (line 143). So the report-injection / bounded out-of-tree disclosure is real.

The claim is NOT a hallucination and is NOT already guarded: notably the codebase itself recognizes this exact threat elsewhere. go/internal/scanner/textscan/textscan.go:99 explicitly skips symlinks with the comment "Prevents loops and silent privilege boundary crossings (e.g. /tmp symlink to /etc)" — but that protection is applied only in the Go textscan walker, not in the Python AST analyzer (engine.py:80-87 invokes ASTAnalyzer with no path sanitization) nor in the Go secrets per-file read. So the "accepted tradeoff" defense fails for this specific code path: the same project deliberately defends against it in a sibling scanner.

Severity remains low (not higher) for grounded reasons: (1) the leak is constrained — content only reaches `evidence`/`taint_chain` when a line matches a narrow dangerous-call regex (eval/exec/innerHTML/SQL-template on the JS side; eval/os.system/subprocess/execute/etc. on the Python side), and is capped at ~200 chars per matching line; it is not an arbitrary full-file read. (3) The realistic precondition (scanning attacker-controlled content) is supported: docs/github-app.md and docs/ci-cd-integration.md document a first-class "clone the PR head → run fendix scan" workflow, so a malicious fork PR can plant the symlink — this is what keeps it a genuine (low) finding rather than refuted.

An operator who only scans first-party code never hits this. The exposure is also opportunistic: it requires an out-of-tree file that both exists/readable on the runner AND contains a line matching a sink regex, and yields only ~200 chars per matching line rather than full-file contents. surviving.title: Workflow-wide contents:write + packages:write + id-token:write granted to all release jobs, including ones that don't need them
surviving.description: The `permissions:` block is declared once at workflow scope (lines 8-13) granting contents:write, packages:write, and id-token:write to every job: enforce-signing, release, publish, docker, and mirror. - publish (L364-370) uses softprops/action-gh-release with GITHUB_TOKEN — needs only contents:write.
- docker (L387-392 GHCR login + L444-537 cosign) needs packages:write + id-token:write, not contents:write.
- mirror (L539-746) operates entirely against a different repo (Abdel-RahmanSaied/homebrew-fendix) via secrets.DIST_REPO_TOKEN PAT (L578, L669, L713) and never references the workflow GITHUB_TOKEN — needs none of the three scopes.

This is a genuine least-privilege deviation from GitHub's documented guidance (scope permissions to the minimum, ideally per-job). The blast-radius reasoning is correct: scoping per-job would contain a compromised go-install tool (nfpm L99, syft L192/L470 are version-pinned via the module proxy, not SHA-pinned — a real supply-chain vector) so it could not mint OIDC tokens AND push to GHCR AND write repo contents simultaneously.

However the claimed medium severity overstates direct exploitability. The trigger is `on: push: tags: v*` (L3-6), not PR/fork, so there is no untrusted-fork code-injection path; an attacker needs push-write to tag or a separate dependency compromise. All third-party actions are SHA-pinned (L57, L61, L144, L340, L365, L382-412, L547-550), neutralizing the finding's "tag-moved tool/poisoned action" example. The heredoc predicate interpolations (L291, L504) only interpolate trusted GITHUB_* context and matrix values, not attacker-controlled input, so they are not the injection points the finding implies. The author also explicitly reasoned about id-token:write (L11-12 comment). Net: a valid defense-in-depth hardening gap contingent on a separate compromise, not a directly exploitable flaw — low.
surviving.falsePositiveRisk: The condition is real and matches the code exactly, so it is not a false positive in the factual sense. The "false positive" angle is severity inflation: GitHub Actions GITHUB_TOKEN is auto-scoped to the triggering repo only and is short-lived; the dangerous-looking packages:write/contents:write apply solely to this repo, and the most sensitive operations (mirror) use a separate PAT that the workflow-wide permissions do not affect at all. With SHA-pinned actions and a tag-only trigger, there is no first-party injection path, so the practical exposure is limited to a hypothetical compromise of a version-pinned go-install tool — defense-in-depth, not an active vulnerability.

surviving.title: Untrusted finding fields rendered raw into PR-comment Markdown (report/markdown injection)
surviving.description: RenderPRComment writes finding.Severity, finding.Title, and the endpoint/line value directly into Markdown with fmt.Fprintf (comment.go:141) and into a YAML code fence via suppressionSnippet (comment.go:146-147, 71-82). These finding fields ultimately derive from scanning attacker-controlled repo content (file paths, matched strings become titles/endpoints). No escaping of Markdown/HTML control characters is applied to Title or endpoint before they land in the comment body that PostPRComment posts to the Issues API (comment.go:171-208). The suppression snippet %q-quotes endpoint/category for YAML (line 80) but Title is not quoted there and Title/endpoint are not escaped in the bullet line (141).
surviving.impact: A crafted filename or code snippet that becomes a finding Title/endpoint can inject Markdown/HTML into the App's PR comment — e.g. break out of the code fence, inject a misleading link, or spoof additional fake findings/'✅ no findings' text to socially engineer a reviewer into merging. GitHub sanitizes raw HTML in comments, limiting XSS, so impact is content-spoofing rather than script execution; hence low.
surviving.recommendation: Escape Markdown metacharacters (backticks, pipes, brackets, newlines) in Title and the where value before interpolation, and ensure code-fence content cannot contain a closing fence. Consider rendering untrusted strings inside inline-code spans with backtick-count escaping.
surviving.verifierReasoning: Re-read go/internal/ghapp/comment.go. Line 141 `fmt.Fprintf(&b, "- **[%s]** %s — `%s`\n", f.Severity, f.Title, where)` writes finding.Title and the endpoint/line (`where`, set from f.Endpoint or f.Line at 137-139) raw into the PR-comment Markdown body with no escaping of backticks, newlines, or Markdown/HTML metacharacters. The body is then JSON-marshaled and POSTed by PostPRComment (171-208) to the Issues comments API as the App, so the rendered comment carries the App's trust. Attacker-controllability is confirmed by the project's own threat model docs/threat-model.md T7 (273-300), which explicitly classifies finding Title and Endpoint as attacker-controlled (reflected payloads from target responses) and requires html.EscapeString in the HTML reporter with fixtures for
surviving.falsePositiveRisk: Most first-party blackbox scanner Titles are static literal strings (e.g. "CORS wildcard origin with credentials allowed"), so Title injection requires the plugin path or a finding whose Endpoint reflects an attacker-controlled path/URL; the highest-signal injection vector in practice is the endpoint/`where` value, not Title. The description also overstates the suppressionSnippet sink (Title is hashed there, not rendered raw). GitHub's GFM HTML sanitization caps impact at content-spoofing, and exploitation needs the attacker to control repo content/plugin output that the scanned org chose to run, which somewhat reduces real-world likelihood. The endpoint is %q-quoted inside the YAML fence (line 80), so that specific sub-channel is partially mitigated, leaving line 141 as the unescaped sink.

surviving.title: python/requirements.txt uses floating >= lower-bounds with no upper bound or hash pinning
surviving.description: All six runtime deps are pinned as `>=` lower bounds (semgrep>=1.45.0, bandit>=1.9.4, pyyaml>=6.0.3, openapi-spec-validator>=0.9.0, detect-secrets>=1.5.0, packaging>=26.2) with no upper bound and no `--hash` pinning. This file is installed into the Docker images (Dockerfile:42-44, Dockerfile.app:53-55) via `pip install -r` and in CI (ci.yml:61, heavy-eval.yml:58), and pyyaml here parses untrusted .fendix.yaml / OpenAPI specs (per dependabot.yml:58-60 rationale). With `>=` and no hashes, every fresh build resolves to whatever newest version PyPI serves — builds are non-reproducible and a compromised/yanked-and-republished or typosquat-adjacent upstream release is pulled silently. The SLSA/SBOM provenance is generated from the Go binary, but the Python engine deps (which ship in the Docker image and run the analyzers) are not pinned to exact versions or hashes.
surviving.impact: Non-deterministic Docker/CI builds and an open window for a malicious upstream Python release to enter the runtime image that runs analyzers over untrusted PR code (see ghapp finding). Undermines reproducibility claims and the value of the SBOM, since the SBOM reflects a moving target. Dependabot does cover pip (dependabot.yml:67-77) but only opens bump PRs; it does not pin the floor to a verified artifact.
surviving.recommendation: Pin exact versions (==) and add hashes (pip-compile --generate-hashes / a requirements.lock) installed with `pip install --require-hashes`. Bound the major versions to avoid silent breaking/major bumps, and ensure the Docker images install from the hashed lockfile.
surviving.verifierReasoning: Re-read the actual files; every load-bearing claim holds. /Users/asaied/WorkDir/Fendix/fendix-engine/python/requirements.txt lines 1-6 are exactly: semgrep>=1.45.0, bandit>=1.9.4, pyyaml>=6.0.3, openapi-spec-validator>=0.9.0, detect-secrets>=1.5.0, packaging>=26.2 — all floating `>=` lower bounds, no upper bound, no `--hash`, and no --require-hashes. There is no lockfile/constraints file anywhere in python/ (only requirements.txt, 112 bytes). Installation sites confirmed: Dockerfile lines 42-44 (COPY python/requirements.txt + pip install --no-cache-dir -r), Dockerfile.app lines 53-55 (same), .github/workflows/ci.yml lines 60-61 (pip install -r requirements.txt), .github/workflows/heavy-eval.yml line 58 (pip install -r python/requirements.txt). So every fresh build resolves to whatever PyPI serves at build time — builds are genuinely non-reproducible for the Python layer, and the SBOM/SLSA provenance (built from the Go binary, FROM lines digest-pinned, go.sum committed) does not cover these moving Python versions. This is NOT an accepted/documented tradeoff: docs/threat-model.md T6 lines 223-224 under "Dependency hygiene" explicitly states "python/requirements.txt pins exact versions" — that claim is false, so the code violates a documented invariant rather than honoring one, which strengthens the finding. Dependabot does cover pip (dependabot.yml lines 67-77) but only opens bump PRs; it neither pins a floor to a verified artifact nor adds hashes, so reproducibility is unaffected. Two minor framing corrections that do not refute: (1) the finding cites dependabot.yml lines 58-60 as pyyaml rationale, but that comment is in the gomod block and refers to gopkg.in/yaml.v3 (Go), not pyyaml — the broader fact that the engine parses untrusted YAML/OpenAPI still stands; (2) severity is real but bounded: exploitation needs an upstream compromise/yank-republish/typosquat of one of six well-known packages, and dependabot plus CI test runs give partial detection, so "low" is the right grounding despite the aggravating doc contradiction.
surviving.falsePositiveRisk: The packages are mainstream and dependabot/CI provide partial monitoring, so the open window is narrow in practice; an enterprise may accept floating floors as a deliberate "stay-current" posture. Also the specific dependabot.yml:58-60 citation in the description actually describes the Go yaml.v3 dep, not pyyaml, which slightly weakens the stated untrusted-parsing chain for the Python side (though the engine does parse untrusted input via these deps). None of this negates the literal, verified facts: floating >= bounds, no hashes, installed into images/CI, and a threat-model statement that falsely claims exact pinning.

surviving.title: Release mirror job uses a broad cross-repo PAT (DIST_REPO_TOKEN) to clone, force-rebase, and push to a public install repo
surviving.description: The mirror job authenticates to the public homebrew-fendix repo with secrets.DIST_REPO_TOKEN, a static PAT embedded into a clone URL (line 581 `https://x-access-token:${GH_TOKEN}@github.com/${MIRROR_REPO}.git`) and used for a bounded rebase+push loop (lines 688-709) and `gh release create/upload` (lines 711-745). This token writes the very artifacts users install (Formula/fendix.rb with SHA256s, install.sh, the released binaries on the mirror). Putting the PAT in the remote URL means it is written into .git/config inside the runner workspace; combined with `set -eu` heredoc generation it is generally redacted by Actions, but a PAT is long-lived vs the workflow GITHUB_TOKEN. The job also regenerates Formula/fendix.rb by interpolating ${{ steps.sha.outputs.* }} into a heredoc (lines 589-648) — if a SHA output were ever attacker-influenced it would land in the published formula.
surviving.impact: A leaked or over-scoped DIST_REPO_TOKEN (or a compromised step in this job, which inherits the workflow-wide write perms) grants persistent write to the public distribution repo — the single highest-value supply-chain target, since it serves install.sh and the binaries every `brew install`/curl|sh user trusts. A static PAT is harder to rotate and broader than a scoped GitHub App token.
surviving.recommendation: Replace the PAT with a fine-grained token scoped to contents:write on only homebrew-fendix, or a GitHub App installation token minted per-run. Avoid embedding the token in the remote URL (use a credential helper / `git config http.extraheader` with masking). Add per-job `permissions: {}` so the mirror job doesn't also carry the workflow GITHUB_TOKEN write scopes it doesn't use.
surviving.verifierReasoning: Every cited line exists exactly as described in /Users/asaied/WorkDir/Fendix/fendix-engine/.github/workflows/release.yml. The `mirror` job (lines 539-746, `needs: publish`, MIRROR_REPO=Abdel-RahmanSaied/homebrew-fendix) authenticates to the public install repo with `secrets.DIST_REPO_TOKEN` exposed as GH_TOKEN. Line 581 embeds the token in the clone URL `https://x-access-token:${GH_TOKEN}@github.com/${MIRROR_REPO}.git`; lines 688-709 are a bounded (max_attempts=5) rebase+`git push origin HEAD:main` loop; lines 711-745 run `gh release create/upload` against $MIRROR_REPO with the same token. Lines 589-648 regenerate Formula/fendix.rb via heredoc. The factual substrate of the finding is fully accurate, and the mirror repo genuinely is the highest-value supply-chain endpoint (serves install.sh, the Homebrew formula with SHA256s, and the binaries every brew/curl|sh user trusts). Severity is correctly LOW, and I would not raise it, for these reasons: (1) Embedding the token in the clone URL is the canonical GitHub-documented HTTPS auth pattern; the secret is log-redacted by Actions and .git/config lives only in the ephemeral runner — the finding itself concedes "generally redacted," so this is not a defect. (2) The SHA values interpolated into the formula come from read_sha (lines 564-566) reading dist/*.sha256 produced by the trusted same-run build matrix that is gated behind enforce-signing + cosign — there is no attacker-influenced path; the finding hedges this with "IF a SHA output WERE ever attacker-influenced," a conditional with no realized primitive. (3) Using a cross-repo PAT is the only mechanism to push to a separate repo (the default GITHUB_TOKEN cannot write cross-repo), so this is necessary by design, not a misconfiguration; the "inherits workflow-wide write perms" framing conflates GITHUB_TOKEN with the PAT, which is the only credential doing the cross-repo writes. The net residual finding is a valid hardening recommendation — prefer a scoped GitHub App token or fine-grained PAT over a static long-lived PAT — which is real and appropriately rated low.
surviving.falsePositiveRisk: The "broad cross-repo" scoping claim is unverifiable from the repository: DIST_REPO_TOKEN is a GitHub secret whose actual permissions (it may already be a single-repo fine-grained PAT scoped only to homebrew-fendix) cannot be inspected from code, so "broad" is an assumption. Pushing to a separate public repo necessarily requires a non-default credential, making the PAT usage required-by-design rather than a flaw. The two speculative sub-claims (SHA injection into the formula, .git/config token leakage) have no realized exploit path and could be dropped entirely. The finding is best read as a defensible hardening/best-practice note, not an exploitable vulnerability.

surviving.title: Scan report metadata Version is hardcoded to "dev" — every SARIF/PDF/JSON report misreports the tool version
surviving.description: The orchestrator receives the real build version (NewOrchestrator(cfg, version) -> o.version, :47-62) and uses it for the debug bundle (bundle.Write(o.version) :503), but sets report metadata Version: "dev" as a literal (:441) instead of o.version. meta.Version flows into SARIF driver.version (sarif.go:295), the PDF footer/version row (pdf.go:66,253), and JSON report version (json.go:17).
surviving.impact: Every released binary emits reports claiming version "dev". This breaks SARIF provenance in Code Scanning/Defender, audit-trail reproducibility (which build produced this report?), and any downstream baseline keyed on tool version; it also makes cross-release regression triage impossible from the report alone.
surviving.recommendation: Set Version: o.version (fall back to "dev" only when empty) at orchestrator.go:441. NewOrchestratorWithSpawner (:66) doesn't set version — populate it there too so test/embedder paths don't regress to empty.
surviving.verifierReasoning:
Re-read the cited code and the full data flow; the finding is accurate.

1. orchestrator.go:437-446 builds `meta := reporters.ScanMetadata{...Version: "dev"...}` with `Version` hardcoded to the string literal "dev" (line 441), NOT `o.version`.

2. The orchestrator holds the real build version: `NewOrchestrator(cfg, version string)` sets `o.version = version` (orchestrator.go:47-62), and the caller passes the build-injected value: `cmd/fendix/main.go:354` -> `engine.NewOrchestrator(cfg, Version)`.

3. `Version` is set at build time via ldflags, confirmed across the build system: Makefile:31 (`-X main.Version=$(VERSION)`), .github/workflows/release.yml:86 (the release path, `-X main.Version=${VERSION}`), and Dockerfile:35 (`-X main.Version=docker`). So for any released/Docker binary the real value is a semver/tag, not "dev" — ruling out "it's always dev anyway." (reporters/parse.go:30 even asserts an expected parsed version of v0.4.1.)

4. The inconsistency is proven two lines apart: the debug bundle correctly uses the real value — `bundle.Write(o.version)` (orchestrator.go:503) — while the report metadata uses the literal. The fix is a one-liner: `Version: o.version`.

surviving.falsePositiveRisk: The hardcoded "dev" could be an intentional placeholder if the team treats report-embedded version as non-authoritative (relying on the `fendix version` CLI subcommand or release artifact name for provenance instead). It is also possible some non-release build paths leave Version="dev" anyway, but the release.yml and Dockerfile injections show the production path does set a real value, so the misreport is real for shipped binaries. Severity is bounded: this is a metadata-correctness defect with no exploit primitive, which is why it is low rather than medium for a security review.

surviving.title: No panic recovery in scanner worker pool or finding-decode loops — a panic on adversarial input aborts the whole scan
surviving.description: WorkerPool.Run launches worker goroutines calling job.check() directly with no recover() (:64-90); there is zero recover() in non-test code (grep confirmed). Scanner checks parse attacker-controlled data (target HTML/JS/headers, OpenAPI specs, osv.dev JSON). A panic in any check (nil deref, slice bounds, regex on malformed input) propagates and crashes the process — no report, non-graceful exit. The Python spawner and plugin readers likewise lack recover around decode loops.
surviving.impact: In the CLI, a scan against a hostile/malformed target becomes a crash with no report (the exit-code contract never runs). The same scanner path runs inside the GitHub App via the `fendix scan` subprocess against arbitrary PR contents, so a crafted PR could reliably crash scans. Recovering per-job (mark check failed, continue) is standard for a tool ingesting untrusted input concurrently.
surviving.recommendation: Wrap each job.check call in a deferred recover() that logs the panic with endpoint/check context and returns nil for that job. Do the same around plugin/Python decode loops. Add an adversarial-input/fuzz test asserting no panic escapes a check.
surviving.verifierReasoning: The code claims are accurate. workerpool.go:62-91 spawns wp.workers goroutines whose body is `for job := range jobs { ...; findings := job.check(ctx, cfg, job.endpoint); ... }` with no defer/recover (verified verbatim at lines 64-90). `grep -rn "recover()" go/ --include=*.go | grep -v _test.go` returns empty — there is zero panic recovery in any non-test code, and orchestrator.go / cmd/fendix/main.go / internal/cli have no defer-recover either. The architectural point is correct and load-bearing: in Go a panic in ANY goroutine terminates the whole process, and a recover() in the calling function (pool.Run / orchestrator.Run) cannot catch a panic that originates in a worker goroutine — so the only fix is a per-worker recover. The blast radius claim holds: orchestrator.go:189-190 builds the pool and calls pool.Run, and a worker panic would skip the `return 2` exit-code contract and abort with no report written. The attacker-controlled-input + GitHub-App reachability claims are also real: CheckHeaders reads response headers, probeSQLi/probeSQLiErrorBased scan response bodies, and deps/{govulncheck,pip,npm} decode osv.dev/govulncheck JSON; ghapp/scanner.go:125 runs `fendix scan --code <dir>` as a subprocess against arbitrary PR contents (deps scanners are always-on for --code, the GH App's path), so a crash there is captured as a generic scan failure with no findings/SARIF (scanner.go:131-133). This is a legitimate defense-in-depth/availability gap, so it is not refuted. I downgrade severity from medium to low because the finding does not demonstrate any concrete panicking code path — it asserts generic "nil deref / slice bounds / regex on malformed input." The actual ingestion uses Go stdlib net/http, encoding/json (into typed structs), and regexp, all of which are panic-safe on malformed input; injection body-parsing (the most aggressive surface) is additionally gated behind --enable-active. So a crash requires a latent bug to already exist in some check; the impact is real if such a bug exists, but exploitability today is speculative rather than proven. It is a robustness hardening item, not a confirmed remotely-triggerable crash.
surviving.falsePositiveRisk: No specific panicking code path is identified; the named panic classes (nil deref, slice bounds, bad regex) are not demonstrated against any actual check, and the stdlib parsers used (net/http header access, encoding/json into typed structs, regexp) do not panic on adversarial/malformed input. The riskiest body-parsing check (injection) is gated behind --enable-active and is not on the default or GitHub-App scan path. Thus the finding may be a theoretical defense-in-depth gap with no presently-reachable crash, making the "reliably crash scans" impact claim unsubstantiated as written.

surviving.title: Embedded-Python-engine code path and user-facing messages are stale after the embedded distribution was dropped
surviving.description: Post-TASK-118 the default scan is Python-free and the embedded Python distribution was dropped (orchestrator.go:328-333; models/config.go:95-103). Accumulating drift erodes trust in the CLI's self-documentation and inflates support load.

Every cited code location exists verbatim and the described drift is real and uncorrected by any guard.

Two of those three named checks no longer use Python: native Go packages internal/scanner/secrets/ (TASK-115) and internal/scanner/semgrep/ (TASK-116) exist, and orchestrator.go:275-311 runs them unconditionally when CodePath is set, BEFORE and independent of the Python block. The comment at line 277 even states secrets "runs unconditionally... regardless of Python availability." So the message misnames secrets/semgrep as Python-dependent.

2. embedded.go still declares //go:embed all:engine, HasEngine(), and ExtractEngine(). But the only producer of that engine/ dir — the Makefile embed-engine target — now deliberately resets it to a single .gitkeep placeholder ("Python engine no longer bundled — TASK-118"). Therefore in release builds HasEngine()==false, ExtractEngine errors with "no embedded engine files," and `fendix engine sync` returns "this binary has no embedded engine."

3. cmd/fendix/engine.go:34-37 still advertises the engine as "normally bundled with the binary and extracted on first scan" — false for default release builds. Impact is limited to mildly misdirecting an operator during support triage. surviving.title: SARIF invocation.executionSuccessful is hardcoded true even when scanners partially failed (fail-open)

At minimum surface partial-failure in JSON report metadata so CI can distinguish 'clean' from 'incomplete'.

The SARIFInvocation struct (sarif.go:101-104) has only ExecutionSuccessful and CommandLine — there is no toolExecutionNotifications field, confirming failures cannot be surfaced. ScanMetadata (json.go:13-22) carries Target/StartedAt/Duration/Version/Mode/EndpointsCount/ActiveProbes/ChecksRun — no field for scanner-failure state, so partial-failure cannot be threaded into the render even if RenderSARIF wanted it. The orchestrator's continue-on-error pattern is confirmed at the exact lines cited: native go deps slog.Warn at 215, pypi at 244, npm at 271, secrets at 289, semgrep at 310, textscan at 321 — each on a default (non-sentinel) error path that logs and continues. A grep for any failure-tracking identifier (ScanErrors/PartialFail/toolExecutionNotification) returns only the two hardcoded sites. sarif_test.go:421-423 asserts executionSuccessful is always true, confirming this is locked-in behavior. So the technical claim holds: a dep-CVE scan whose OSV.dev/network call fails produces zero findings for that ecosystem yet emits executionSuccessful=true with no notifications, which a SARIF consumer (GitHub Code Scanning) reads as 'ran clean / no vulns' rather than 'scanner failed' — a real fail-open for a SARIF-driven CI gate. Severity stays low: there is no attacker-controlled input (it is a reporting-fidelity gap, not the claimed report-injection vector — nothing is injected), failures are still visible via slog.Warn on stderr, and triggering harmful impact requires an infrastructure failure to coincide with an operator relying solely on the SARIF invocation status while ignoring stderr. The category label 'report-injection' is also a misfit; this is fail-open / missing error propagation, not injection. surviving.title: Ignore-file parse failure and save-baseline errors are logged but don't affect exit code (silent fail-open in CI)
surviving.description: When --ignore is set but the file fails to parse, the orchestrator logs slog.Error and proceeds with no suppression applied (:398-405); SaveBaseline failure only logs (:450-452). Neither propagates 'the operator asked for X and X failed' into the exit code — exit is driven purely by checkFailOn. By contrast, discovery and report-render failures correctly return exit 2.
surviving.impact: In CI a typo in .fendix-ignore (or a bad baseline path) is a silent error buried in logs: the build proceeds, suppressions silently don't apply (or a relied-upon save-baseline silently doesn't happen). For a gating tool, 'the config you provided was invalid' should be a hard, visible failure, not an INFO-buried log that still exits 0/1 as if everything worked.
surviving.recommendation: Treat an explicitly-provided-but-unparseable --ignore or a failed --save-baseline as exit code 2 (configuration error), consistent with policy-load and report-render handling. At minimum print the error to stderr (not just slog) so it's visible in default CI log capture.
surviving.verifierReasoning: Code matches the finding exactly. At orchestrator.go:398-405, when o.cfg.IgnorePath != "" and ParseIgnoreFile fails (os.ReadFile error or yaml.Unmarshal error, per ignore.go:30-38), the orchestrator logs slog.Error("failed to parse ignore file...") and the if/else has no else-branch action beyond skipping ApplyIgnoreRules — so findings is returned unchanged and Run continues. No suppression is applied and the exit code is unaffected. At orchestrator.go:449-452, SaveBaseline failure (json.Marshal or os.WriteFile error, per baseline.go:49-60) only logs slog.Error and continues; the requested baseline silently does not get written. By contrast, discovery failure (line 138), no-endpoints (line 157), and report-render failure (line 462) each return 2. The exit code is the CI gate: main.go:355-358 passes orch.Run's int straight to os.Exit. There is NO upstream validation — main.go:218/224 read --save-baseline/--ignore as raw strings and place them directly into ScanConfig (lines 284-287) with no os.Stat or syntax pre-check. The inconsistency is sharpened by the fact that the explicit --config policy path IS validated (main.go:264-268: "refuse to silently fall back to flag-only" when the operator points at a nonexistent file), so the same "operator explicitly asked for X" principle is honored for policy but not for ignore/baseline. So the finding's factual claims (cited code exists, behavior is fail-open, contrast with exit-2 paths is real, no guard handles it) all hold. This is correctly a maintainability/robustness issue, not a security vulnerability: it is not attacker-controllable (an adversary does not control the operator's local .fendix-ignore content or the --save-baseline directory in CI), and there is no threat-model doc accepting or rejecting this case (threat-model.md does not mention ignore/baseline error handling). Real impact is an operator-misconfiguration footgun in a gating tool — a typo in .fendix-ignore or an unwritable baseline path degrades silently behind an slog.Error that does not change exit 0/1. Low severity is accurate and arguably generous (borderline info), since it requires operator error and has no confidentiality/integrity/availability consequence for the scanned target.
surviving.falsePositiveRisk: Could be deemed accepted design rather than a defect: the codebase has a deliberate "log-and-continue" posture for many subsystems (native dep/secrets/semgrep scan failures slog.Warn and continue; plugin failures continue; ApplyBaselineDiff on a bad --baseline also only logs and returns current). One could argue the ignore/save-baseline handling is intentionally consistent with that resilience philosophy — "never let an auxiliary step abort the scan." Also, slog.Error (not Warn/Info) is used, so in a default INFO-level CI run the message IS visible on stderr at ERROR level, partially mitigating the "buried in logs" framing; the description's claim that it is "INFO-buried" is slightly inaccurate (it is logged at ERROR). The defect is therefore the missing exit-code propagation, not log visibility.

surviving.title: Plugin env redaction uses substring match on prefixes, redacting unrelated vars and missing some secret shapes
surviving.description: redactPluginEnv drops any env var whose NAME contains any entry in secretEnvPrefixes via strings.Contains (line 89), despite the field being named 'prefixes' and the doc claiming a prefix check. This is a substring match: it over-redacts (e.g. a benign `MY_TOKEN_BUDGET` is dropped because it contains `TOKEN`) and is order/spelling dependent. More importantly it is a denylist — any credential-bearing var whose name does not contain one of the listed fragments (e.g. `STRIPE_KEY` does not contain API_KEY/SECRET/TOKEN; `SENTRY_DSN`; vendor-specific names) is passed through to third-party plugin code. The redaction is a useful mitigation but should not be relied on as the security boundary, especially given the plugin code-execution exposure noted in plugin-entrypoint-symlink-worldwritable-trust.
surviving.impact: Credential leakage to third-party plugin subprocesses for any secret env var not matching the denylist; plus surprising behaviour where legitimate non-secret config is stripped. Informational because the dominant risk is the plugin executing at all (covered separately).
surviving.recommendation: Switch to an allowlist model: pass only an explicit set of env vars the plugin manifest declares it needs (the FX-PLUG-2 follow-up the comment references), plus PATH/HOME/locale. If keeping a denylist, match on true prefixes (strings.HasPrefix) and document it as best-effort, not a boundary.
surviving.verifierReasoning:
The cited code exists exactly as described. plugin.go:88-91 does `for _, p := range secretEnvPrefixes { if strings.Contains(name, p) { continue NEXT } }`, a case-sensitive SUBSTRING match on the var name, despite the slice being named `secretEnvPrefixes` (line 52). The list (lines 52-68) is a denylist: API_KEY/SECRET/TOKEN/PASSWORD/etc. So the finding's two core technical claims are both true: (a) over-redaction — `MY_TOKEN_BUDGET` is dropped because it contains `TOKEN`; (b) denylist gaps — `STRIPE_KEY`, `SENTRY_DSN`, and arbitrary vendor secret names whose substrings aren't listed pass through to the plugin subprocess (cmd.Env at lines 307-310 calls redactPluginEnv(os.Environ())).

However, the finding's framing that the doc 'claims a prefix check' while the code silently does substring matching is refuted by the actual code. The behavioral doc comment on redactPluginEnv (lines 70-74) accurately states: 'The match is a case-sensitive substring check on the variable's *name*, not value, so a custom `MY_SECRET_THING=...` is dropped (matches `SECRET`)'. The package-level comment (lines 47-51) says 'The list intentionally over-redacts'. And env_redaction_test.go:74-86 (TestRedactPluginEnv_TokenSubstringIsRedacted) explicitly pins the substring/over-redaction behavior: 'This is intentional over-redaction; the test pins the contract.' So the substring behavior and over-redaction are documented, tested, and deliberate — a known/accepted design tradeoff, not an undocumented defect.

The denylist-incompleteness concern is real and correctly identified, but the redaction is explicitly positioned in-code as best-effort defense-in-depth, not the security boundary, and the finding itself concedes the dominant risk is plugin code-execution (covered by plugin-entrypoint-symlink-worldwritable-trust). The only undocumented gap is the misleading `secretEnvPrefixes` identifier name vs. substring semantics — a minor maintainability nit. Net: technically accurate observations, but it is a documented/accepted tradeoff with no incremental security boundary being claimed, so info severity stands and it is effectively known/duplicate of the separately-tracked plugin-execution risk.
surviving.falsePositiveRisk: The denylist-completeness gap (e.g. STRIPE_KEY passing through) is a genuine residual exposure, so a reviewer could legitimately keep this as a low-value info item rather than dismiss it. The substring behavior, however, is provably intentional (documented in the behavioral doc comment and pinned by a dedicated test), so the 'silent mismatch between prefixes naming and substring behavior' angle is largely a false positive — only the identifier name is misleading, the behavior is documented.

surviving.title: Installation token passed to many call sites; error strings from GitHub API include response bodies
surviving.description: PostPRComment and UploadSARIF (sarif.go:72-74) build error strings that embed the GitHub API response body verbatim (responseBody from io.ReadAll(LimitReader(...))). These errors bubble up through handler.runScan -> HandlePullRequest and are logged via ctx.Logger.Error('event handler failed', 'err', err) in webhook.go:150. The installation token itself is sent only in the Authorization header (not in the URL) for these two calls, so it is not directly echoed; however, GitHub error bodies can reflect request context, and the same err wrapping pattern is used in the scanner's git step (scanner.go:114 uses redactToken there, but comment.go/sarif.go do NOT apply any token redaction to the bubbled error). If a future change moves the token into a URL/query or a body field, these unredacted error paths would leak it into operator logs.
surviving.impact: Currently low — token is header-only for these calls so no direct leak. The risk is the inconsistency: scanner.go defensively redacts tokens from error strings while comment.go/sarif.go do not, making it easy for a future edit to introduce a token-in-log leak. GitHub error bodies in logs may also reveal repo/installation details.
surviving.recommendation: Apply a consistent token-redaction helper (like scanner.go's redactToken) to all error strings in the ghapp package that may contain credentials, and add a regression test asserting the installation token never appears in any returned error from PostPRComment/UploadSARIF/FetchInstallationToken.
surviving.verifierReasoning:
The cited code exists exactly as described. comment.go:203-206 reads `responseBody, _ := io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(resp.Body, 4<<10))` then `return fmt.Errorf("post comment: %s: %s", resp.Status, string(responseBody))` with no token redaction. sarif.go:72-74 has the identical pattern (`fmt.Errorf("sarif: upload: %s: %s", resp.Status, string(responseBody))`). The asymmetry with scanner.go is real and correctly explained: scanner.go:114 calls redactToken() because injectInstallationToken (scanner.go:174) embeds the token in the git clone URL userinfo, so it CAN appear in git error output; comment.go/sarif.go do not redact because they never put the token anywhere reflectable.

I verified the token is header-only for both calls. In PostPRComment the URL (comment.go:178-180) is `baseURL/repos/owner/repo/issues/N/comments` with no token, and the token is only at line 194 `req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+installationToken)`. The POST body (line 182-184) is the comment markdown. UploadSARIF is the same: URL at sarif.go:55-56, token only in the Authorization header at line 63, body is `{commit_sha, ref, sarif}`. GitHub does not echo the Authorization header back in error response bodies, and neither request body contains the token. Therefore there is NO present path by which the installation token leaks into the error string or the operator log.

The call chain is partly as claimed: PostPRComment's error is wrapped at handler.go:209 (`fmt.Errorf("post comment: %w", err)`), bubbles through HandlePullRequest -> dispatch, and is logged at webhook.go:150 `ctx.Logger.Error("event handler failed", "err", err)`. One correction: the UploadSARIF error does NOT bubble to webhook.go:150 — it is best-effort and logged separately as a Warn at handler.go:219 (`ctx.Logger.Warn("SARIF upload failed", "err", err)`), with the function continuing. Either way the GitHub 4KB-capped error body reaches operator logs.

So the factual claims hold, but the finding describes a HYPOTHETICAL future leak ("if a future change moves the token into a URL/query or body field") and explicitly concedes current impact is "low — token is header-only ... so no direct leak." There is no present secret exposure. What lands in logs is a GitHub error body (repo/installation context, status text), which is operational metadata, not a credential, and is bounded to 4KB. This is a defense-in-depth / code-consistency hardening observation, not a current vulnerability.
surviving.falsePositiveRisk: The finding could be read as a present secret-leak (its category is secret-handling and severity low), but the token provably cannot reach these error strings today: it is sent only in the Authorization header, never in the URL/query/body, and GitHub does not reflect that header in error responses. The "leak" is entirely contingent on a future code change that does not exist. The only present-day effect is GitHub API error bodies (non-secret repo/installation context) appearing in operator logs, which is normal diagnostic behavior. Treating this as a live low-severity secret-handling bug overstates it; it is an info-level hardening/consistency suggestion (apply redactToken defensively in comment.go/sarif.go to match scanner.go).

surviving.title: Arabic locale ships machine-generated, security-unreviewed strings rendered as authoritative report labels; ScanSubtitle placeholder tokens are inert
surviving.description: The Arabic Strings constructor is entirely TRANSLATION_REVIEW_NEEDED (every field, per the header and inline comments) yet is selectable today via --lang ar (i18n.Get / IsSupported return Arabic for 'ar'). These strings are STATIC and developer-controlled (not attacker-influenced) and are auto-escaped by html/template, so this is not a code-injection vector; the risk is correctness/integrity: an unreviewed machine translation of severity labels (SeverityCritical/High) and section headers could mistranslate the severity an operator sees. The ScanSubtitle/i18n strings contain {target}/{mode}/{duration} placeholder tokens (ar.go line 14, en.go line 9), but the HTML template does NOT use ScanSubtitle (the subtitle on html.go line 96 is built from Metadata fields directly), so those tokens are inert and no locale-driven format-string substitution path is reachable.
surviving.impact: An Arabic-language report could display mislabelled severity/section text to an operator who relies on it for triage, before a native-speaker security review clears the baseline. Reputational/correctness risk for an enterprise localisation claim; not an injection or RCE vector.
surviving.recommendation: Gate --lang ar behind a feature flag (or mark it experimental/beta in the CLI and report footer) until the TRANSLATION_REVIEW_NEEDED items are cleared by a native-speaker security reviewer, as the RISKS.md register already anticipates. Either wire the ScanSubtitle placeholder template through a safe substitution that cannot be abused, or remove it from the struct to avoid future misuse.
surviving.verifierReasoning: Every factual claim checks out against the code. ar.go (lines 11-62) marks all fields TRANSLATION_REVIEW_NEEDED, and the doc-comment (lines 3-8) states a native-speaker security reviewer must clear them before public release. i18n.go confirms Get() returns Arabic() for "ar" (lines 86-87) and IsSupported() returns true for "ar" (line 99), so --lang ar is selectable today via the reporters/lang.go re-export. The strings are static Go literals rendered through html/template ({{.I18n.X}} on html.go lines 95-139), so they are auto-escaped, developer-controlled, and not attacker-influenced — there is no report-injection / code-injection / RCE path, exactly as the finding itself concedes. The ScanSubtitle claim is also correct: html.go line 96 builds the subtitle directly from Metadata fields ({{.Metadata.Target}} — {{.Metadata.Mode}} scan — {{.Metadata.Duration}}) and never references {{.I18n.ScanSubtitle}}; a repo-wide grep shows ScanSubtitle is used nowhere outside the constructors and the struct definition, so its {target}/{mode}/{duration} tokens are inert and no locale-driven format-string substitution is reachable. Severity labels (SeverityCritical/High etc., html.go lines 98-102) DO use the I18n strings, so an unreviewed Arabic label is displayed. However: (1) the finding is mis-filed under report-injection while its own description disclaims any injection; (2) the code explicitly documents this as a known, tracked design tradeoff (TRANSLATION_REVIEW_NEEDED markers, RISKS.md reference, gated on v0.13.0-stable promotion); and (3) the spot-checkable Arabic severity values are in fact correct (حرج=critical, عالي=high, متوسط=medium, منخفض=low, معلومة=info), so the "could mistranslate severity" impact is speculative. This is an accepted/documented localization-quality tradeoff, not a security vulnerability. Verdict: known/accepted design tradeoff; severity correctly capped at info.
surviving.falsePositiveRisk: The technical observations are all accurate (verified line-by-line), so it is not a fabricated finding. The reason it is effectively a non-issue is that the code itself documents and tracks this as an intentional pre-release baseline (TRANSLATION_REVIEW_NEEDED markers + RISKS.md register entry gated on v0.13.0-stable), the strings are static and auto-escaped (no injection), and the concrete mistranslation impact is unsupported because the shipped Arabic severity labels are actually correct. It is best treated as a known/accepted design decision rather than an actionable security finding.

surviving.title: Per-endpoint probe cap is a soft/approximate limit — TOCTOU between Count() and the Record() calls allows overshoot
surviving.description: The MaxProbesPerEndpoint cap (default 20) is enforced by checking `auditLog.Count(endpoint.FullURL) >= maxProbes` at the entry of each probe function and at the top of each payload iteration (367, 402, 508, 663, 734). Each check is a separate locked read, but multiple Record() calls happen after it: a single time-based SQLi hit records BOTH the initial probe AND a confirmation probe (lines 441 and 456) before the next Count check, and CheckInjectionWithAudit fires five probe types per target before re-checking at the top of the loop. So the actual probe count for an endpoint can exceed the configured cap by a bounded amount (roughly one target's worth of probes). This is per-endpoint only — concurrent endpoints don't interfere because Count filters by FullURL — but within one endpoint the cap is approximate, not hard.
surviving.impact: An operator who sets --max-probes-per-endpoint as a strict politeness/safety bound (e.g. for a fragile production target under --enable-active) can see meaningfully more probes than configured against a single endpoint, and the audit log / budget telemetry will reflect more probes than the stated cap.
surviving.recommendation: If the cap is meant to be hard, check-and-reserve atomically (e.g. have ProbeAuditLog expose a TryReserve(endpoint) bool that increments under the same lock), or re-check Count immediately before each Record and abort the probe. If it is intentionally soft, document it as 'approximate, may overshoot by up to one target's probe set' in the flag help and the CheckInjectionWithAudit doc comment.
surviving.verifierReasoning:
The core behavior is real and verified. ProbeAuditLog.Count() (injection.go:121-131) and Record() (103-109) are each independently mutex-locked, but the check-then-record sequence is not atomic, so the per-endpoint MaxProbesPerEndpoint cap (default 20) is enforced approximately, not as a hard limit. The concrete overshoot mechanism the finding cites is genuine: in probeSQLi a confirmed time-based hit calls auditLog.Record() twice (lines 441 and 456) after a single Count() guard at line 402, with no intervening Count check (verified lines 438-467). So the recorded probe count for an endpoint can exceed the configured cap.

However the finding both mischaracterizes and overstates the issue:

1) Magnitude is overstated. The claim is "roughly one target's worth of probes" (~5, the five probe types in the CheckInjectionWithAudit loop, lines 372-382). In reality each subordinate probe re-checks the cap itself: probeSQLiErrorBased (508), probeCMDi (663), probeCRLF (734) all return early when Count()>=maxProbes, and probeSQLiBoolean (583) explicitly reserves two slots with `Count()+2 > maxProbes` to avoid its own overshoot. So once the cap is reached the only path that records beyond a passed guard is the SQLi time-based confirmation double-record, which overshoots by exactly +1 — and only when a time-based SQLi actually confirms at the cap boundary. The realistic worst case is the cap+1, not cap+5.

2) The "TOCTOU / concurrency" framing is inaccurate. The orchestrator worker pool (orchestrator.go:185-190) dispatches per (endpoint, check) unit, so a single endpoint's injection probes run sequentially inside one CheckInjectionWithAudit goroutine. Count() filters records by FullURL (line 126), so concurrent endpoints have independent counters and cannot race each other's budget (the finding itself concedes this). There is no data race — Count/Record are mutex-protected — so this is a check-granularity slack, not a concurrency bug. Category "concurrency" is wrong; it is at most an off-by-a-small-bounded-amount accounting issue.

Real-world impact for an enterprise deployment: an operator who sets --max-probes-per-endpoint as a politeness/safety bound under --enable-active (which already requires explicit authorization and prints a disclaimer, lines 51-57, 184) can see at most one extra HTTP probe against a single endpoint, and only on an endpoint that confirms a time-based SQLi. The audit log will faithfully record that extra probe (so telemetry is accurate, not misleading). This is a documented design tradeoff in spirit — the boolean probe shows the authors deliberately chose per-probe guards rather than a hard pre-reservation — and the divergence is +1 in a narrow condition. Behavior confirmed, but the severity is info, not low, and the concurrency/TOCTOU characterization and the magnitude claim are both incorrect.
surviving.falsePositiveRisk: Could be argued as not-a-bug: the cap is a per-probe-checked best-effort budget (the boolean probe's +2 reservation shows intentional design), the overshoot is a deterministic single-goroutine off-by-one rather than a race, and it only triggers on a confirmed-vulnerable endpoint at the exact cap boundary under an already-authorized active scan. The audit log accurately reflects the actual probe count, so there is no telemetry deception.

surviving.title: Malformed UTF-8 is handled (no crash) via errors='replace' — confirmed safe, informational
surviving.description: Both _analyze_python and _analyze_js_heuristic read with errors='replace', so invalid UTF-8 bytes become U+FFFD rather than raising UnicodeDecodeError — the analyzers do not crash on malformed-UTF-8 source files. spec_parser, by contrast, decodes the URL body and reads local files with plain encoding='utf-8' (no errors= argument), so a non-UTF-8 spec would raise UnicodeDecodeError; that is a subclass of ValueError and IS caught by check_auth's except tuple, so it surfaces as SEC-SPEC-PARSE rather than a crash. Recording this as confirmation that the 'crash on malformed UTF-8' concern does not apply to the engine as written.
surviving.impact: None — documents that malformed-UTF-8 inputs are robustly handled across the analyzers, so the Go-side 'crash == scan failure' concern is not triggered by encoding alone.
surviving.recommendation: No change required. For consistency, spec_parser local/URL reads could also use errors='replace', but current behavior correctly degrades to a parse-error finding.
surviving.verifierReasoning: Every claim in this informational finding is verified against the actual code. python/analyzers/ast_analyzer.py line 107 reads `source = filepath.read_text(encoding="utf-8", errors="replace")` inside `_analyze_python`, and line 126 reads the same `source = filepath.read_text(encoding="utf-8", errors="replace")` inside `_analyze_js_heuristic` — matching the cited evidence exactly. Per Python's codec semantics, `errors="replace"` substitutes invalid byte sequences with U+FFFD instead of raising UnicodeDecodeError, so neither analyzer crashes on malformed-UTF-8 source files. The try/except wrappers further harden this: `_analyze_python` catches `(OSError, SyntaxError)` (lines 104-110) and `_analyze_js_heuristic` catches `OSError` (lines 123-128), with both also enforcing a 1 MB `_MAX_FILE_BYTES` size guard before reading. I also verified the secondary comparison: python/analyzers/spec_parser.py line 278 decodes the URL body with plain `resp.read().decode("utf-8")` and line 282 reads local files with `path.read_text(encoding="utf-8")` — neither passes an `errors=` argument, so a non-UTF-8 spec would indeed raise UnicodeDecodeError (a ValueError subclass) rather than yielding U+FFFD; the finding's note that this is caught by check_auth's except tuple and surfaces as SEC-SPEC-PARSE is consistent with that design. This finding is explicitly an informational confirmation that the analyzers robustly handle malformed UTF-8; it asserts the absence of a vulnerability rather than the presence of one. The code fully supports that conclusion. There is no exploitable behavior to refute — the claim is technically correct and the cited lines exist verbatim.
surviving.falsePositiveRisk: Not a vulnerability at all, so there is no exploitability to over- or under-state. The only nuance worth recording: errors="replace" silently corrupting bytes can, in rare cases, cause a downstream secret/pattern regex to miss a match if the secret contained non-UTF-8 bytes, or cause ast.parse to fail on the replaced text and bail via the SyntaxError handler (a quiet skip). That is a detection-completeness/maintainability tradeoff, not a crash or a security hole, and it does not change the info-level verdict.

surviving.title: Reference workflow users copy uses floating action tags and `go install ...@latest`, contradicting the repo's SHA-pin policy
surviving.description: The reference workflow shipped for users to drop into their repos pins everything to floating tags: actions/checkout@v4 (51), setup-go@v5 (53), setup-python@v5 (57), actions/cache@v4 (75), github/codeql-action/upload-sarif@v3 (118), actions/github-script@v7 (129), and installs Fendix itself via `go install github.com/Abdel-RahmanSaied/Fendix/cmd/fendix@latest` (line 67). `@latest` resolves to whatever the newest tag is at run time — no pin, no provenance, and it ignores the entire signed-release/cosign path the project built. This is the template that propagates the project's CI hygiene to every adopter.
surviving.impact: Every downstream repo that adopts the reference workflow inherits floating, un-pinned third-party actions (the exact risk class T6/SECURITY.md warn about) and installs the scanner from an unverified `@latest` build rather than a cosign-verified release. A tag-move on any of those actions, or on the Fendix repo, executes in the adopter's CI with security-events:write + pull-requests:write (lines 42-45). It also undercuts the project's own marketed supply-chain posture.
surviving.recommendation: SHA-pin all actions in the example (with `# vN` comments, matching the internal workflows) and replace `go install ...@latest` with the install.sh + cosign-verify path or a pinned release version. Add a note that adopters should pin to the latest reviewed SHA.
surviving.verifierReasoning: Every cited line is accurate. examples/github-actions/fendix-scan.yml is explicitly a copy-into-your-repo reference template (lines 1-3) and pins all third-party actions to floating major tags: actions/checkout@v4 (L51), setup-go@v5 (L53), setup-python@v5 (L57), actions/cache@v4 (L75), github/codeql-action/upload-sarif@v3 (L118), actions/github-script@v7 (L129), and installs Fendix via `go install github.com/Abdel-RahmanSaied/Fendix/cmd/fendix@latest` (L67). The job grants security-events:write + pull-requests:write (L42-45). The contradiction with stated policy is real and self-documented: docs/threat-model.md §T6 (L214-218) states the project uses "commit-SHA-pinned third-party actions (every uses: line carries a 40-char SHA...)", the project's own .github/workflows/*.yml all SHA-pin (e.g. actions/checkout@de0fac2e...d5 # v6.0.2), and ci.yml L96-97 has a guard that FAILS CI on any floating @vN tag citing §T6 — a guard this reference file would fail. §T6 residual-risk (L230-234) and SECURITY.md (L194, L350-351) both explicitly warn against `go install ...@latest` for production gates, which L67 does. So the finding holds factually and the policy mismatch is genuine. However: severity is overstated. This is a non-executing example template, not Fendix's own pipeline — it has zero impact on the security of a Fendix enterprise deployment itself. Risk only materializes in a third party's CI if they adopt it verbatim and ignore the file's own inline caveat (L61-64) flagging the install path as interim, and the threat-model already classifies this exact case as accepted residual risk. That makes it an informational consistency/hygiene gap, not a low-severity product vulnerability.
surviving.falsePositiveRisk: The "vulnerability" is in a documentation/example artifact, not in any code path that runs as part of Fendix or its release pipeline. The project explicitly documents the @latest install as known residual risk and flags it inline as a temporary measure pending the binary release pipeline (Phase 13/TASK-099), so it is arguably an accepted, documented design tradeoff rather than an oversight. The floating-tag use in a sample workflow may be an intentional readability choice for a template users are expected to customize.

surviving.title: Docker images pin base digests and run as non-root, but install Python deps without hash verification
surviving.description: Positive baseline worth recording: both Dockerfile (golang:1.25-alpine@sha256:8d22..., python:3.14-slim@sha256:7a50...) and Dockerfile.app pin base images by digest (Dockerfile:8,39; Dockerfile.app:17,41), use multi-stage builds, run as a dedicated non-root `fendix` user (Dockerfile:54-55; Dockerfile.app:65-66), use --no-cache-dir and clean apt lists, and Dockerfile.app uses tini for signal handling. No secrets are baked into layers (the App reads secrets from env at runtime). The k8s manifest adds readOnlyRootFilesystem, drop ALL caps, runAsNonRoot, seccomp RuntimeDefault (deploy/k8s/fendix-app.yaml:32-68). The remaining gap is that `pip install -r requirements.txt` (Dockerfile:43, Dockerfile.app:54) inherits the floating/unhashed requirements (see requirements-floating-lower-bounds-no-hashes), so the image layer contents are not reproducible.
surviving.impact: Image base layers are reproducible and the runtime is well-hardened — strong posture. The only residual supply-chain weakness in the image is the unpinned Python dependency layer, tracked separately. No root execution, no digest drift, no baked secrets.
surviving.recommendation: Install the Python engine deps from a hashed lockfile (`pip install --require-hashes`) inside the Dockerfiles so the full image is reproducible and matches the SBOM. Otherwise the Docker supply-chain controls here are a good model.
surviving.verifierReasoning: Every factual claim in this informational/positive-baseline finding checks out against the actual files.
