surviving.title: configleak TLS block is a no-op whose comment claims the opposite behavior
surviving.description: The comment says verification is NOT required, but the code sets InsecureSkipVerify:false (default = verification ON). The transport is budget.Transport() (a *budgetTransport wrapping http.DefaultTransport), so the *http.Transport type assertion fails and the block never runs anyway. Comment, intent, and actual behavior all disagree.
surviving.impact: A reviewer auditing TLS posture is actively misled: comment claims verification disabled, code claims to enable it, neither executes. A trust/maintainability landmine — the next engineer can't tell the intended TLS behavior, and it signals copy-paste cruft likely repeated across the per-check HTTP client blocks.
surviving.recommendation: Delete the dead if-block and contradictory comment. Centralize TLS posture in one shared http.Client/transport factory used by all checks and document plainly whether cert verification is on or off for probes.
surviving.verifierReasoning:
Verified against go/internal/scanner/configleak.go lines 106-115 and go/internal/budget/budget.go lines 126-138.

The three-way contradiction is real:
1. Comment (lines 110-112): "We deliberately don't require TLS verification for the probe itself ... The same posture as the rest of the scanner." => states verification is intentionally OFF.
2. Code value (line 114): `InsecureSkipVerify: false` => that is Go's zero value, meaning verification is ON. This is the literal opposite of what the comment claims.
3. Dead code: line 108 sets `Transport: budget.Transport()`, and `budget.Transport()` returns `WrapTransport(http.DefaultTransport)` which returns `&budgetTransport{...}` (a `*budgetTransport`, see budget.go:130/136-138). The type assertion on line 113, `client.Transport.(*http.Transport)`, therefore always fails (`ok==false`), so lines 113-115 never execute. There is no reassignment of client.Transport between line 108 and line 113, so the assertion can never succeed. Confirmed the block is unreachable.

So comment, code intent, and runtime behavior all disagree, exactly as the finding states. The effective TLS behavior is http.DefaultTransport's default = full certificate verification (verification ON), which happens to match the misleading `false` value but contradicts the comment's stated "don't require TLS verification."

Severity assessment: This is purely a maintainability/comment-rot defect with ZERO security or runtime impact. Importantly, the code does NOT weaken TLS — it does not set InsecureSkipVerify:true and the dead block would not disable verification even if it ran. So there is no MITM/exploitability angle; the scanner correctly verifies TLS via the default transport. The only harm is reviewer confusion. I adjust from low to info because there is no exploitable or behavioral consequence in an enterprise deployment — it is dead, self-canceling code plus a wrong comment.

One sub-claim in the impact is overstated: I grepped the whole scanner package and internal tree (grep for InsecureSkipVerify / client.Transport.(*http.Transport) / TLS verification) and this block appears ONLY in configleak.go. The claim that it is "copy-paste cruft likely repeated across the per-check HTTP client blocks" is not supported by the codebase — no other check contains this block. The core finding (dead, self-contradictory TLS block) is fully confirmed; the "repeated across checks" speculation is refuted.
surviving.falsePositiveRisk: Low risk that the core finding is a false positive — the dead-code and comment-contradiction facts are mechanically verifiable and confirmed. The main caveat is that this is a maintainability nit with no security impact, so anyone treating it as a TLS/security risk would be wrong: the scanner still performs full certificate verification via http.DefaultTransport. Additionally, the "repeated across per-check HTTP client blocks" portion of the impact is a false positive (grep found it only in configleak.go).

refuted.title: Attacker-controlled PR head SHA flows unvalidated into `git fetch origin <SHA>` (argument injection / RCE on the App host)
refuted.description: FendixScanner.Run builds the fetch step as `{gitBin, "-C", dir, "-c", "protocol.version=2", "fetch", "--quiet", "--depth=1", "origin", req.HeadSHA}` and runs it via exec.CommandContext (runCommand, line 178-186). req.HeadSHA originates from the pull_request webhook field `p.PullRequest.Head.SHA` (handler.go:148) / check_run `head_sha` (handler.go:303) and is passed through with NO validation anywhere (grep for HeadSHA shows no hex/length check; scanner.go only checks it is non-empty at line 74). Because the SHA is the trailing positional argument and is never separated from options with `--`, a fork PR whose head SHA string begins with `-` is parsed by git as an option. `git fetch` honours `--upload-pack=<cmd>` (and `--exec=`), which runs an arbitrary command on the host running fetch. So a value like `--upload-pack=touch /tmp/pwn` (or a more useful payload) is executed by the GitHub App server. The same unvalidated value also reaches `git checkout FETCH_HEAD` and the SARIF upload.
refuted.impact: Remote code execution on the Fendix GitHub App host, triggered by opening a pull request from a fork against any repo the App is installed on. The webhook signature check (webhook.go:52) does NOT help here — the payload is legitimately signed by GitHub; the attacker controls the fork content, not the HMAC. The App holds installation tokens for every installed org/repo, so RCE here is a full multi-tenant compromise.
refuted.recommendation: Validate HeadSHA against `^[0-9a-fA-F]{7,64}$` before use and reject otherwise. Additionally pass `--` before positional refs (`fetch ... origin -- <SHA>` is not valid for fetch; instead fetch by refspec or validate strictly). Apply the same hex validation in handler.go where HeadSHA is extracted from both pull_request and check_run payloads.
refuted.verifierReasoning: The code-level claims are mostly accurate. scanner.go:108-109 builds `{gitBin, "-C", dir, "-c", "protocol.version=2", "fetch", "--quiet", "--depth=1", "origin", req.HeadSHA}` with req.HeadSHA as the TRAILING POSITIONAL arg and NO `--` end-of-options separator. There is no format validation of HeadSHA anywhere in the package (verified via grep: no regexp/hex/length/HasPrefix check); the only guard is the non-empty check at scanner.go:74 and handler.go:168, and TestFendixScanner_Run_ValidatesInputs (scanner_test.go:191-204) confirms a non-SHA string like "x" is accepted. The value originates from the HMAC-signed webhook JSON (handler.go:148 p.PullRequest.Head.SHA, handler.go:303 p.CheckRun.HeadSHA) and flows unmodified into the fetch step. Commands run via exec.CommandContext (no shell), so the only in-scope risk is git argument injection, which the finding correctly identifies — and `git fetch --upload-pack=<cmd>` does execute arbitrary commands. So a missing-validation / argument-injection hardening gap genuinely exists.\n\nHOWEVER the critical RCE claim is refuted on exploitability. The headline attack ("open a fork PR whose head SHA string begins with `-`, e.g. --upload-pack=touch /tmp/pwn") cannot be realized: GitHub populates pull_request.head.sha and check_run.head_sha with a genuine Git commit object ID composed solely of hex characters [0-9a-f] (40 chars for SHA-1, 64 for SHA-256). A fork PR author controls commit CONTENT but cannot cause GitHub to serialize a non-hex, dash-prefixed string into that field of a legitimately HMAC-signed webhook. Because no value beginning with `-` can reach req.HeadSHA via normal GitHub webhook delivery, git never parses it as an option, and the --upload-pack RCE path is not triggerable in practice for an enterprise deployment. The finding also contains a factual error: it claims "the same unvalidated value also reaches git checkout FETCH_HEAD," but scanner.go:110 passes the literal string \"FETCH_HEAD\", not the SHA. This is a real defense-in-depth defect (add a `--` separator and a hex/length validator), but it is latent — exploitable only if an upstream/MITM actor with the webhook secret, a compromised GitHub Enterprise instance, or a future code path fed a crafted SHA — not a fork-PR-triggered critical RCE. Severity adjusted from critical to low.
refuted.falsePositiveRisk: If a deployment ever sources HeadSHA from a less-trusted channel (a manual/admin re-scan endpoint, a queue, GitHub Enterprise with a tampered API, or an attacker who has obtained the webhook secret and can forge signed payloads), a `-`-prefixed value could reach git and the argument-injection-to-RCE becomes real. The missing `--` separator and missing hex validation are objectively present, so a future refactor that introduces such a source would silently turn this into a true critical. It should be fixed as hardening even though the currently-described fork-PR attack path is not viable.

refuted.title: Installation token embedded into attacker-controlled fork clone_url (no host allowlist) → token exfiltration / SSRF
refuted.description: HandlePullRequest selects the clone URL as `p.PullRequest.Head.Repo.CloneURL` first, only falling back to the repository's own clone_url (handler.go:135-138). For a fork PR, head.repo.clone_url is the FORK's URL, which the attacker fully controls. injectInstallationToken (scanner.go:166-176) parses it and, after checking ONLY that the scheme is `https`, embeds the short-lived installation token as `https://x-access-token:<token>@<attacker-host>/...` and `git remote add origin` uses it (line 107). There is no allowlist that the host is github.com / the configured GHES host. git then makes an outbound authenticated request to the attacker host, sending the installation token in the Basic-auth userinfo (and on HTTP redirect git may forward it). This is both SSRF (App makes git/https requests to an attacker-chosen host, including internal addresses) and credential exfiltration of a token scoped to the installation.
refuted.impact: An external attacker who opens a fork PR can cause the App to leak an installation access token to an arbitrary host they control, then replay it against the GitHub API for the duration of the token's life — escalating to write access on the victim org's repos. Even absent a host they control, the unrestricted host enables SSRF to internal/metadata endpoints via git's https transport.
refuted.recommendation: Pin the clone host to the configured GitHub host (api.github.com / GHES host derived from BaseURL). Prefer using `p.Repository.CloneURL` (the base repo the App is installed on) rather than the fork's head.repo.clone_url for the authenticated fetch; fetch the fork's commit via the base repo's `refs/pull/<n>/head` or `refs/pull/<n>/merge` which GitHub exposes on the base repo. Never embed the token into a URL whose host is not on the allowlist.
refuted.verifierReasoning:
The code mechanics are exactly as cited. injectInstallationToken (scanner.go:166-176) validates ONLY u.Scheme == "https" and embeds the token as userinfo with no host allowlist; HandlePullRequest (handler.go:135-138) selects cloneURL := p.PullRequest.Head.Repo.CloneURL first, falling back to p.Repository.CloneURL; Run() git remote add origin uses the authed URL (scanner.go:107) and git fetch (scanner.go:108-109) would send the userinfo as HTTP Basic auth to whatever host is in the URL. So far the finding is accurate.

The finding fails on its core exploit precondition: "head.repo.clone_url is the FORK's URL, which the attacker FULLY controls." It is not. The webhook body is HMAC-SHA256 verified against FENDIX_WEBHOOK_SECRET before any parsing (webhook.go:129-138), and the clone_url field is populated by GitHub from the actual repository record, not by raw attacker bytes. For a genuine external fork PR, GitHub renders head.repo.clone_url as https://github.com/<attacker>/<repo>.git (or the operator's fixed GHES host) — the SCHEME and HOST are GitHub-controlled; the attacker controls only the fork's owner/name path segment and its contents. An external attacker cannot make a GitHub-signed pull_request webhook carry head.repo.clone_url = https://attacker.evil/ or https://169.254.169.254/. Producing such a payload requires forging the HMAC, i.e. possessing the webhook secret — and an attacker with the secret already has full control of the App and a far worse primitive than this.

Consequently the two claimed escalations are not reachable via the stated attack (an external fork-PR opener):
1. Token exfiltration to an arbitrary attacker host — unreachable; the host is fixed to github.com / the configured GHES host by GitHub. For a real fork the token is sent only to github.com, which is the token's legitimate intended audience; GitHub enforces installation scope server-side (the fork is not in the installation, so the fetch simply fails auth or behaves as unauthenticated for a public fork). No third party receives the token.
2. SSRF to internal/metadata endpoints — unreachable for the same reason; the destination host cannot be steered away from github.com / GHES via a fork PR.

What remains is a legitimate but defense-in-depth-only gap: there is no explicit allowlist asserting u.Host == github.com (or the configured GHES host) before embedding the token. This matters only under preconditions outside the claimed threat (leaked webhook secret, a future code path sourcing clone_url from a less-trusted input, or a compromised/hostile GHES instance) — none of which the finding establishes. The high/medium claim overstates real exploitability because it assumes byte-level attacker control of a GitHub-signed, GitHub-populated field. Adjusted to low (hardening recommendation: add a host allowlist in injectInstallationToken or before remote add).
refuted.falsePositiveRisk: If a deployment ever sources the clone URL from a less-trusted channel than the HMAC-verified GitHub webhook (e.g., an internal API, a queue, or a GHES instance the org does not fully trust), or if the webhook secret is weak/leaked, the missing host allowlist becomes directly exploitable as described, making it a real token-exfil/SSRF primitive. The hardening (host allowlist) is genuinely worth doing; the refutation is specifically of the claimed external-fork-PR exploit path and its high severity, not of the code smell itself.

refuted.title: Install URL allowlist accepts scp-style strings beginning with '-' (argument-injection surface into `git clone`)
refuted.description: validateInstallURL permits scp-style URLs via validInstallURLScpRe = `^[A-Za-z0-9_.-]+@[A-Za-z0-9_.-]+:[A-Za-z0-9_./-]+$`. The first character class includes '-', so a value such as `-x@host:path` passes validation and is then handed to gitClone as the `srcURL` positional in `exec.Command("git", "clone", "--depth=1", srcURL, destDir)` (line 220) with no `--` separator. git parses a leading-dash argument as an option. While `-x@host:path` is not a known git-clone option (git errors out) and the better-known dangerous transports (`ext::`, `file://`) are correctly rejected, the allowlist still lets a `git`-option-shaped token reach argv. This is operator-supplied input (the user types the URL), so impact is limited to self-inflicted; nonetheless it defeats the stated intent of the allowlist.
refuted.impact: Low in the current CLI usage (the operator chooses the URL). Becomes meaningful if `plugins install` is ever driven by a less-trusted caller (registry flow, automation). At minimum it is an argument-injection foothold into git clone.
refuted.recommendation: Insert `"--"` before srcURL and destDir in gitClone: `exec.Command("git", "clone", "--depth=1", "--", srcURL, destDir)`. Also tighten validInstallURLScpRe to require the first character to be alphanumeric (e.g. `^[A-Za-z0-9][A-Za-z0-9_.-]*@...`).
refuted.verifierReasoning: The factual premise is correct but the security claim does not hold. Confirmed in /Users/asaied/WorkDir/Fendix/fendix-engine/go/internal/pluginscmd/pluginscmd.go: line 143 validInstallURLScpRe = `^[A-Za-z0-9_.-]+@[A-Za-z0-9_.-]+:[A-Za-z0-9_./-]+$` includes '-' in the leading class, and line 220 calls exec.Command("git","clone","--depth=1",srcURL,destDir) with no `--`. I verified in Go that `-x@host:path`, `-ufoo@host:bar`, and `--upload-pack@host:path` all match the regex, and that git parses such a leading-dash token as an option (e.g. `-ufoo@host:bar` is consumed as --upload-pack). However, NO consequential argument injection is reachable: the char class before '@' forbids '=', '/', space, and ';', so the dangerous options that need a value or separator (--upload-pack=, -c key=val, -o) cannot be formed in a single glued token. The one option that does take a glued value, -u/--upload-pack, only triggers helper execution after a transport connection is established; but runInstall guarantees destDir (~/.fendix/plugins/<name>) does NOT exist before clone (stat check lines 265-269), so git takes destDir as the repo positional and dies with "repository ... does not exist" before any transport/upload-pack runs. I confirmed empirically that `git clone --depth=1 -utouch@x:y /nonexistent` executes nothing and exits with a fatal error. Thus the worst outcome is git printing a usage/fatal error that runInstall surfaces as "git clone failed" — no code execution, no file read, no boundary crossed. The allowlist's documented intent (comment lines 123-140) is specifically to block code-EXECUTING transports file:// and ext::, which ARE rejected and pinned by TestValidateInstallURL_RejectsDangerousTransports (which already covers --upload-pack=evil and ext::). A leading-dash scp token is not such a transport, so the stated intent is not defeated. Trust model is explicitly operator-supplied/self-inflicted (package doc lines 10-15: "The community installs plugins by URL and trusts what they install"); install is a CLI-only subcommand (lines 183-213) with no less-trusted caller — the hypothesized registry/automation flow is documented as a non-existent future Q3 candidate. This is at most a cosmetic input-hygiene gap / defense-in-depth nit, not a vulnerability.
refuted.falsePositiveRisk: If a future change ever (a) drives `plugins install` from a less-trusted caller (registry/automation), AND (b) loosens the scp regex to permit '=' or '/' before '@', AND (c) allows the dest to be a pre-existing local repo, the missing `--` separator could become a real argument-injection vector. Adding `--` before srcURL is a cheap, correct hardening and would make the finding moot. So while refuted today, the underlying "no -- separator" observation is a legitimate hardening suggestion worth noting as info.

refuted.title: pip-audit subprocess passes discovered manifest path without `--` separator
refuted.description: scanViaSubprocess runs `exec.CommandContext(ctx, pipAuditPath, "--format", "json", "-r", m)` where `m` is a requirements.txt path discovered by filepath.WalkDir under the (absolute) scan root (findRequirementsManifests, lines 599-629). The path is preceded by the `-r` flag, so it is consumed as that flag's value rather than as a standalone positional — meaning a leading-dash filename does not by itself smuggle a new option here. The residual risk is defensive: the manifest path is derived from filesystem contents (which, for the GH App flow, come from an untrusted cloned repo) and is passed to a third-party tool without a `--` guard, and pip-audit's own flag parsing for the value of `-r` is relied upon. No exploit is demonstrated; flagged for hardening only.
refuted.impact: No concrete exploit identified given the `-r <value>` positioning. Defense-in-depth gap if pip-audit's argument handling changes or if a future refactor passes the manifest positionally.
refuted.recommendation: Add a `"--"` terminator before the manifest path and/or assert that `m` has the `.../requirements.txt` basename and an absolute, in-tree path before invoking pip-audit. Same hardening applies anywhere a filesystem-derived path is passed to a subprocess.
refuted.verifierReasoning: Re-read go/internal/scanner/deps/pip/scanner.go. Line 525 is exactly `cmd := exec.CommandContext(ctx, pipAuditPath, "--format", "json", "-r", m)` followed by `cmd.Output()`. This is NOT a command-injection vector: Go's exec.Command/CommandContext pass arguments directly to execve as a discrete argv slice with no shell, no word-splitting, and no metacharacter/glob expansion. A manifest path containing spaces, `;`, `$()`, backticks, or pipes is delivered to pip-audit as a single literal argv element, so OS command injection is structurally impossible here irrespective of any `--` separator. The finding itself concedes there is no exploit and that the `-r <value>` positioning prevents option-smuggling (argparse consumes the next token as the flag's value). Two additional guards further reduce even the theoretical residual risk: (1) pipAuditPath is resolved via exec.LookPath("pip-audit") at line 214 — the executed binary is trusted and not attacker-controlled, only the `-r` value is repo-derived; (2) findRequirementsManifests (lines 599-629) only appends a path when `d.Name() == "requirements.txt"` (line 619), so the basename is always exactly "requirements.txt" and can never begin with a dash — meaning even the speculated "future refactor passes it positionally" scenario would receive a leading-segment-controlled-only path whose basename is fixed. The feature is also opt-in (opts.UsePipAudit at line 213). The claimed command-injection category does not hold; this is at most a stylistic hardening nit relying on a tool's documented `-r` semantics. Refuted.
refuted.falsePositiveRisk: The hardening observation is technically real (no `--` separator is passed), so a reviewer optimizing for defense-in-depth could argue for adding one. But it is not exploitable: no shell, argv passed directly to execve, trusted binary path, and the manifest basename is hard-constrained to "requirements.txt", so even the positional-refactor hypothetical cannot produce a dash-leading argument from the filename itself.

refuted.title: Diagnostic bundle redacts debug.log but writes probes.jsonl without secret redaction
refuted.description: In Bundle.Write(), redactSecrets(...) is applied only to the debug.log entry (line 277: logText := redactSecrets(b.logBuf.String(), secrets)). The probes.jsonl entry (lines 248-273) is marshalled straight from scanner.ProbeRecord values and written verbatim — no redactSecrets pass. ProbeRecord.Endpoint (injection.go:71) and ProbeRecord.Payload carry per-request endpoint/payload data. In apikey-query auth mode (models/auth.go AuthTypeAPIKeyQuery, ApplyToRequest writes the secret into req.URL.RawQuery, lines 123-130), the credential lives in the URL/query string, so any endpoint label or payload derived from the full URL would carry the secret into probes.jsonl uncredacted. The bundle README explicitly promises the bundle is 'safe to share with maintainers' and that 'any literal occurrence of either credential anywhere inside the slog stream or finding evidence' is redacted — probes.jsonl is neither, so the promise is not upheld for that file.
refuted.impact: An operator who shares a --debug-bundle tarball (the documented bug-report workflow) may leak an apikey-query credential, or any other secret that lands in a probe endpoint/payload, to whoever receives the bundle (a GitHub issue attachment, per the README). Silent credential disclosure outside the trust boundary.
refuted.recommendation: Run probes.jsonl bytes through redactSecrets(secrets) before writeEntry, identical to debug.log. Better: marshal each ProbeRecord, redact the resulting line, then append. Also consider redacting the endpoint/URL surfaces (query strings) at probe-record creation time so the secret never enters the in-memory audit log.
refuted.verifierReasoning:
The mechanical claim in bundle.go is accurate but harmless: in Bundle.Write() (bundle.go:248-274) probes.jsonl is marshalled verbatim from scanner.ProbeRecord with no redactSecrets pass, while debug.log IS redacted (line 277). However, the finding's exploit chain — that the apikey-query credential reaches probes.jsonl via an "endpoint label or payload derived from the full URL" — does not hold against the actual code.

I traced every ProbeRecord construction site (injection.go:417, 456, 523, 636, 678, 756 — the only sources, confgrep'd). In all of them: (1) Endpoint = endpoint.FullURL, and (2) Payload = a canned literal (p.Payload, sqliErrorPayload, cmdiPayload, crlfPayload, or the canned `payload` arg).

endpoint.FullURL is a stored string built at crawl time (crawler.go:306,311: `baseURL + substitutePathPlaceholders(path, schemas)`) — it never contains the auth credential. The apikey-query secret is injected ONLY into the live *http.Request's URL.RawQuery by addAuth (injection.go:826-832: `q.Set(header, cfg.Auth.Value); req.URL.RawQuery = q.Encode()`) and by AuthContext.ApplyToRequest (auth.go:123-130). Crucially, addAuth is always called AFTER the request is built, and it mutates the request object's URL — it never writes back to the stored endpoint.FullURL string. The ProbeRecord captures endpoint.FullURL (the pre-auth, credential-free string), NOT req.URL.String() after auth was applied. So the apikey-query credential is structurally incapable of reaching any ProbeRecord field, hence cannot reach probes.jsonl. The README's "Probe payloads ... not secrets" and the unredacted endpoint label are both factually credential-free for the alleged path.

The Payload field is likewise just the canned attack strings (e.g. "' AND SLEEP(5)--"), matching the README's stated non-secret content.

The only way a credential lands in FullURL is if the operator embeds it directly in --url (e.g. https://user:pass@host) — but that is an explicitly documented, accepted tradeoff in the same README ("If you scan a target whose URL itself contains credentials, the URL is not auto-redacted. Inspect config.json before sharing.") and is not the apikey-query mechanism this finding alleges. The finding's own wording is hypothetical ("any endpoint label ... derived from the full URL WOULD carry the secret"), and that derivation does not occur in the code.
refuted.falsePositiveRisk: There is a narrow, separate, and explicitly-documented residual: if an operator embeds credentials directly in the --url / spec server URL (basic-auth-in-URL form), those propagate into baseURL -> FullURL -> probes.jsonl unredacted, and config.json's redaction would not cover it either. But the bundle README pre-empts exactly this in its "What is NOT redacted" section, making it an accepted design tradeoff, not the apikey-query disclosure the finding describes. So while "probes.jsonl is unredacted" is literally true, the specific credential-leak exploit the finding builds is not reachable.

refuted.title: Secret redaction is naive substring ReplaceAll — misses encoded/split forms and can mask only partially
refuted.description: redactSecrets does strings.Contains + strings.ReplaceAll for each known secret string. This only catches the verbatim cleartext of cfg.Auth.Value (and its Bearer/Basic-stripped form). It does not catch: (a) any transformed representation of the credential — base64-encoded, URL-encoded (%XX), percent-escaped in a query string, or JSON-escaped — which is exactly the form a credential takes once it has been put into an HTTP request URL/body/header and then logged; (b) credentials the operator passed via FENDIX_AUTH that are split across log fields; (c) the GitHub App webhook secret or installation tokens (not part of ScanConfig, so secretsFrom never collects them — but those are CLI-scan secrets, separate trust domain). secretsFrom only handles Bearer/Basic prefixes; an apikey or cookie value with surrounding context (e.g. 'Cookie: session=...; other=...') is added whole, so a substring of the cookie that the log emitted differently won't match. The result is a redactor that gives a false sense of completeness.
refuted.impact: Debug bundles can ship a credential in a form the redactor doesn't recognize (e.g. URL-encoded in a logged request line, or base64 in a Basic header that the scanner re-encoded). Operators trust the bundle is clean and forward it externally.
refuted.recommendation: Redact by structured field at the point of logging rather than post-hoc substring scrubbing — never log the raw Value (use AuthContext.RedactedHeader()/Redacted()). The fetched ref is then checked out and scanned, and the process holds a live installation token.
refuted.impact: A crafted webhook (the signature is the only gate, but a webhook delivered through GitHub for an installed repo is legitimately signed) with a malicious head_sha could turn `git fetch` into an attacker-influenced git invocation on the fendix-app host (Fly.io machine / k8s pod) that runs with the installation token in memory. Even short of RCE, it can cause the fetch to target an attacker upload-pack endpoint. Confidence is medium because exploitability depends on the exact git version's option parsing and that head_sha normally comes from GitHub's own payload.
refuted.recommendation: Validate HeadSHA against a strict hex-of-expected-length regex before use and reject otherwise. Add `-c protocol.allow=never` for `ext`/`file` and pass `--end-of-options` (or `--` where supported) so a leading-dash ref can't be parsed as a flag. Apply the same validation in HandleCheckRun (handler.go:303).
refuted.verifierReasoning:
The data-flow premise is accurate: req.HeadSHA comes unvalidated from the webhook (handler.go:148 p.PullRequest.Head.SHA and handler.go:303 p.CheckRun.HeadSHA), there is no ^[0-9a-f]{40,64}$ check anywhere in internal/ghapp (grep confirmed), and it is passed as a positional arg to `git -c protocol.version=2 fetch --quiet --depth=1 origin <HeadSHA>` (scanner.go:108-109) with no `--` end-of-options separator. I confirmed on git 2.51.0 that git fetch DOES parse dash-prefixed tokens appearing after the remote name (TEST 2: `--exec=foo` yielded "unknown option", proving the parser does not stop at the remote). So the argument-injection *parsing* premise is real.

However the claimed IMPACT (RCE / redirecting the fetch to an attacker upload-pack endpoint on the host holding the installation token) is not achievable, for several independent reasons that refute the medium command-injection severity:

1) No shell — runCommand uses exec.CommandContext with an arg slice (scanner.go:178-179). The attacker controls exactly ONE argv token (the HeadSHA string) and cannot split it. Option forms needing a separate value token, e.g. `--upload-pack <path>`, are therefore unreachable; only joined `--opt=value` single-token forms are.

2) The cited `--upload-pack` vector is structurally closed. `--upload-pack` sets the upload-pack path on the REMOTE end and causes LOCAL execution only over ssh/file/local transports. injectInstallationToken hard-rejects any non-https scheme (scanner.go:171-173), so transport is always HTTPS. Empirically over HTTPS with the pinned protocol.version=2 (and even without it), `--upload-pack=touch /tmp/.../PWNED` produced `warning: setting remote service path not supported by protocol` and was ignored — no process spawned, no file created (TESTS 1, 3, 6).

3) Reviewing the full `git fetch` option set (TEST 5), no other single-token, value-joined option produces local code execution or arbitrary local file clobber from one attacker-controlled token over HTTPS. `--negotiate-only` errors; `--filter`/`--negotiation-tip`/`-o`/`--refmap`/`--shallow-exclude` are transport-side or need a second token.

4) Precondition: GitHub's own webhook payloads always carry a valid 40/64-char hex SHA. To inject a malformed head_sha an attacker must forge the JSON body behind a valid HMAC (VerifySignature in webhook.go), i.e. already possess the webhook secret. The signature is not merely "the only gate" for a benign payload — it is the gate that prevents an attacker from supplying arbitrary head_sha values in the first place.

Realistic worst case: a HeadSHA beginning with `-` makes git fetch fail with "unknown option", runScan returns an error, and that one scan is not processed — a self-contained, single-event denial of one scan. That is a low-severity hardening gap (the fix is trivial: validate the SHA format or add `--` before the refspec), not a medium command-injection/RCE vulnerability. Adjusting to low.
refuted.falsePositiveRisk: If a future change ever permits non-HTTPS clone URLs (e.g. ssh:// or file:// for self-hosted/test setups) OR removes the protocol.version=2 pin, the `--upload-pack=` single-token vector could become locally exec-capable, turning this into a genuine RCE. The missing validation is a real latent weakness even though it is not currently exploitable; the low rating reflects current exploitability, not the absence of a defensive fix. Also, my git-version testing was on 2.51.0; older git versions theoretically differ, but the HTTPS-transport and single-token constraints hold regardless of version, so the structural refutation stands.
